name: Afghanistan
tax: Bitcoin is banned here, so there is no lawful way to hold bitcoin and report gains. The Taliban-run central bank banned bitcoin trading in 2022 and repeated in April 2024 that no online exchange licences have been issued (Crypto Adventure, August 2026).
banking: Banks cannot help with bitcoin. Bitcoin trading is banned, and since 2021 sanctions and frozen reserves have cut Afghanistan off from most of the international banking system, making transfers and cash withdrawals hard (Crypto Adventure, August 2026; Policy Circle).
legal: Bitcoin is banned or very heavily restricted. The Taliban banned bitcoin trading in August 2022 (Wikipedia).
residency: Moving here is not realistic for foreigners. The country is under Taliban rule, is cut off from much of the world's financial system and ranks among the least peaceful countries in the world (Global Peace Index 2026).
spending: There is nowhere to openly spend bitcoin. Bitcoin is banned, police have closed bitcoin businesses and arrested traders, and on-chain activity fell by more than 99% after 2021 (Crypto Adventure, August 2026).
community: There is no visible bitcoin community. Since the 2022 ban, when police shut bitcoin exchanges in Herat and arrested their staff, we found no public bitcoin groups, meetups or events (Blockworks; Crypto Adventure, August 2026).
privacy: Bitcoin is banned or very heavily restricted in Afghanistan, so any bitcoin activity carries legal risk and is closely watched.
stability: Unstable: weak rule of law, a fragile economy and a high risk of sudden changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.31, ranked 142 of 143 countries. Currency: the afghani has held up thanks to aid cash shipments and strict currency controls, but the country is largely cut off from global banking. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 3.106, ranked 156 of 163 countries.
summary: Hostile in all eight areas.

name: Albania
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate. Bitcoin gains and business income from bitcoin assets are taxed at 15% (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Banking works, and you can fund exchange accounts in lek or euros by bank transfer or card, but expect source-of-funds questions about bitcoin money. Many people in Tirana also trade through P2P platforms or cash deals, which can make it harder to show a clean paper trail later. (Newhedge)
legal: Individuals can own and trade bitcoin freely, though it is not legal tender. Albania's 2020 law on financial markets based on distributed ledger technology (Law 66/2020) means bitcoin platforms need a licence from the Financial Supervisory Authority, which approved its licensing rules in 2022 and regularly warns the public about unlicensed platforms, as it did in June 2025. (Financial Supervisory Authority; A2 News 2025; Shufti Pro)
residency: Moving here is easy and affordable for most people. The digital nomad visa needs an income from about €400–815 a month and can be renewed (Global Citizen Solutions; Immigrant Invest).
spending: We found no reports of shops in Albania that regularly accept bitcoin. People mainly buy and hold it through exchanges, P2P trades or a few bitcoin ATMs rather than spending it. (Newhedge)
community: There is a small but real community. Around 38,000 people, about 1.4% of the population, are estimated to own bitcoin, and Tirana has hosted bitcoin events such as the Bitcoin Pizza Day party in May 2025, though we found no sign of a large regular bitcoin meetup. (Newhedge; Unlock Protocol event page)
privacy: Albania has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Bitcoin gains are still taxed, so you need to declare them yourself.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.49, ranked 87 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.725, ranked 36 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for residency. Weakest area is spending.

name: Algeria
tax: Bitcoin is illegal, so there is no lawful gain to tax. Since July 2025, Law No. 25-10 bans owning, buying, selling, mining and promoting bitcoin, with fines of 200,000 to 1,000,000 dinars and up to one year in prison. (Law No. 25-10, 2025; Unlock Blockchain 2025)
banking: Banks cannot handle bitcoin. Since Law No. 25-10 took effect in July 2025, any bitcoin-related transfer is illegal and can lead to prosecution, and strict currency controls already limit sending money abroad. (Law No. 25-10, 2025; Lightspark 2025)
legal: Bitcoin is banned. Law No. 25-10, in force since 24 July 2025, makes it a crime to hold, buy, sell, store, mine or even promote bitcoin, with prison terms of two months to one year and fines of up to 1,000,000 dinars. (Law No. 25-10, 2025; Unlock Blockchain 2025)
residency: Foreigners usually need a job with an Algerian employer and a work permit, or a family tie, to get a residence card. There is no investor or digital nomad visa. (Algerian Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Rivermate 2025)
spending: Nowhere openly accepts bitcoin. We found no shops, and the 2025 ban makes accepting it a crime. (Law No. 25-10)
community: We found no public bitcoin meetups. Since 2025 even promoting bitcoin online is a crime, so any activity is hidden. (Meetup listings 2026; Unlock Blockchain 2025)
privacy: Bitcoin is banned or very heavily restricted in Algeria, so any bitcoin activity carries legal risk and is closely watched.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.49, ranked 88 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.053, ranked 90 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for residency and stability. Weakest areas are tax, banking, legal freedom, spending, community and privacy.

name: American Samoa
tax: American Samoa runs its own income tax system modelled on the US tax code, and bona fide residents pay local tax instead of US federal tax on local income. Bitcoin is generally treated as property, so gains are taxable, but local rules differ from the mainland and are less clear (American Samoa Tax Office; IRS Publication 570).
banking: The territory has a very small banking market with only a couple of local banks, so options are limited, but US citizens and nationals can use US online banks and US-regulated exchanges for on- and off-ramps (IRS; FDIC).
legal: Owning, self-custody and using bitcoin is legal under the US framework; exchanges and payment firms must follow US federal rules, but individuals face no special limits (FinCEN).
residency: American Samoa controls its own immigration, so even US citizens need an entry permit, and other foreigners generally need a local sponsor such as an employer or relative to stay long-term (American Samoa Immigration Office).
spending: We found no shops that accept bitcoin, so there is effectively nowhere to spend it.
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups or visible bitcoin groups in the territory.
privacy: US federal rules apply here, so bitcoin brokers report trades to the US tax office (IRS). These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in American Samoa, that is American Samoa's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the US dollar. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Andorra
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. The top personal income tax rate is 10%, and it applies to bitcoin gains (Cointelegraph).
banking: Andorra's big banks now serve bitcoin users directly. MoraBanc was approved in February 2024 to hold and trade digital assets for clients and offers a way to bring bitcoin profits back into the bank, and Creand Crèdit Andorrà lets its retail customers buy bitcoin from their bank account through Onyze, which the Andorran Financial Authority licensed in June 2025. Expect thorough source-of-funds checks, as everywhere in Andorran banking. (CriptoNoticias 2024; Finect 2025; Alto Andorra)
legal: Individuals can hold, trade and self-custody bitcoin freely. Law 24/2022 on digital assets, passed on 30 June 2022, sets the rules, and companies that hold or exchange bitcoin for others need authorisation from the Andorran Financial Authority, as Onyze received in 2025. (Andorran Banking; Finect 2025)
residency: Moving here is possible, but you will need a good income or savings. Passive residence needs a €48,500 refundable deposit with the Andorran Financial Authority plus income or health conditions. A digital nomad permit is around €3,000 a month (IMI Daily; destivity).
spending: We found no reports of shops, restaurants or hotels in Andorra that regularly take bitcoin. Banks now let you buy and hold it, but paying with bitcoin in daily life is not something you can count on.
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community. Crypto Mondays Andorra runs a relaxed monthly networking meetup at a coworking space in Andorra la Vella, and its first event drew about 75 people, though it covers bitcoin in general rather than bitcoin only. (Crypto Mondays Andorra on Luma)
privacy: Andorra has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Andorra also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Very stable. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: Andorra uses the euro as its official currency under a monetary agreement with the EU in force since 2012. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: a clear digital assets law has been in place since 2022. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Andorra offers a 10% maximum tax on bitcoin gains, banks that now let clients buy and hold bitcoin, a clear digital-asset law and excellent stability. Residency needs a sizeable deposit, and places to spend bitcoin are scarce.

name: Angola
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are cautious and there is no licensed local route for buying bitcoin. A 2024 law bans bitcoin mining and limits the circulation of virtual currencies not issued by a central bank, so most people rely on peer-to-peer trading (Ver Angola 2024).
legal: Bitcoin is restricted. In February 2024 parliament passed a law banning bitcoin mining and related services nationwide and limiting the circulation of virtual currencies not issued by central banks. Simply holding bitcoin is not clearly addressed (Ver Angola 2024).
residency: Moving to Angola is hard unless you have a job offer or a very large investment. The investor (privileged) visa starts at around 5 million US dollars and is assessed by the national investment agency, and permanent residence is discretionary (IBN Immigration Solutions 2026).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. We found no reports of shops in Angola taking it as payment (Ver Angola 2024).
community: There is an online group, Bitcoin Angola, with about 29,000 members that has been active for several years and spoke out against the mining ban, but we found no regular in-person bitcoin meetups (Ver Angola 2024).
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Angola, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.42, ranked 113 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.955, ranked 77 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax. Weakest area is spending.

name: Anguilla
tax: Anguilla has no income tax, no capital gains tax and no estate tax for individuals, whether resident or not, so bitcoin gains are not taxed. The only deductions are social security and a stabilisation levy on wages or self-employed earnings, not on investment gains. (Deloitte Anguilla tax highlights 2026)
banking: Banking works and there are no foreign exchange controls, but Anguilla is a small market and keeping bank relationships has been hard enough that the island runs a special company scheme to help businesses hold on to them. Expect careful source-of-funds checks for bitcoin-linked money. (Trident Trust)
legal: Individuals can hold and self-custody bitcoin freely. Businesses that exchange, transfer or store bitcoin for other people need a licence from the Anguilla Financial Services Commission under the Digital Assets Business Act, 2023; holding coins for yourself is not covered. (Digital Assets Business Act, 2023; Anguilla Financial Services Commission)
residency: The clearest route is permanent residency for people who own Anguilla property worth at least US$750,000, under the Economic Residence Act as amended in July 2024. Without that kind of investment, a job or family ties, moving here is hard. (Anguilla Focus, July 2024)
spending: We found no news reports of shops or restaurants in Anguilla accepting bitcoin, so expect to pay in local currency or US dollars in daily life.
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups or local bitcoin groups in Anguilla. The community, if any, is very small and informal.
privacy: Anguilla has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Anguilla also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for tax and privacy. Weakest areas are residency, spending and community.

name: Antigua and Barbuda
tax: Antigua and Barbuda has no personal income tax and no capital gains tax, so individuals pay nothing on bitcoin gains.
banking: Banking is the weak spot. The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank urges people to treat bitcoin as high-risk, we found no local bank openly offering bitcoin services, and Caribbean banks are under pressure from international partner banks to avoid risky clients.
legal: Antigua and Barbuda has adopted the regional bitcoin law drafted by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which requires bitcoin businesses to register. Individuals are free to use bitcoin.
residency: Antigua and Barbuda offers citizenship by investment from about $230,000, one of the more affordable programmes in the Caribbean.
spending: We found no recent data on businesses accepting bitcoin, and the regional central bank discourages using bitcoin for payments.
community: There is a small bitcoin-curious community, but we found no bitcoin conferences or community projects planned for 2026.
privacy: Antigua and Barbuda has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Antigua and Barbuda also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 38th out of 143 countries, and the Eastern Caribbean dollar is firmly tied to the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Antigua and Barbuda offers zero tax, affordable citizenship and good privacy. Banking for bitcoin users and everyday bitcoin use are both limited.

name: Argentina
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate. Realised gains are taxed at about 5–15% above certain thresholds, after the scheme for declaring bitcoin wealth was removed (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Banks are wary of bitcoin, so moving money in and out can be difficult. In 2022 the central bank barred banks from offering bitcoin services, so fintech apps and person-to-person trading are widely used (Wikipedia).
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. Bitcoin companies must register with the CNV, the national securities regulator, and the central bank barred banks from offering bitcoin in 2022 (soulbit.io; Wikipedia).
residency: Moving here is easy and affordable for most people. The digital nomad (rentista digital) visa needs around $1,000 a month (destivity; digitalnomadsmagazine).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities, where there are visible clusters of businesses. Acceptance is growing but not universal, and the number of businesses is modest compared with the leading countries (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: Argentina has one of Latin America's biggest bitcoin communities. Buenos Aires hosts LABITCONF, the region's largest bitcoin conference; the 2026 edition runs on 30–31 October and includes free self-custody help. The NGO Bitcoin Argentina runs regular meetups in Buenos Aires, and there are bitcoin events in other cities such as Córdoba and Mendoza. (DiarioBitcoin 2026; Luma; CriptoNoticias)
privacy: Argentina has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2029 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Argentina, that is Argentina's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.54, ranked 65 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.922, ranked 71 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for residency and community. Weakest area is banking.

name: Armenia
tax: Armenia has no special bitcoin tax. Private individuals who are not trading as a business generally pay no tax on bitcoin gains, but when an Armenian company buys bitcoin from an individual it must withhold 10% of the amount, and frequent trading can be treated as business income. Rules are still evolving, so keep records (Armenian Tax Code Article 150; Legelata 2024; Armenian Lawyer 2025).
banking: Armenian banks work normally, but they cannot offer bitcoin services directly and must use separately licensed companies, and big international exchanges are not licensed locally. Most people use cards or peer-to-peer trades, and large transfers can attract source-of-funds questions (Central Bank of Armenia; Armenian Lawyer).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. Regulated under the Law on Crypto Assets (2023), Central Bank of Armenia licensing. Individuals free (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: Moving here is comparatively easy. EU and US citizens can stay visa-free for up to 180 days a year, and many remote workers get a one-year renewable temporary residence permit by registering as an individual entrepreneur, which is cheap and takes days, with permits usually issued in 30–60 days (Repat Armenia 2026; Ministry of Foreign Affairs).
spending: Only a handful of places in Yerevan accept bitcoin, and most bitcoin payments that do happen use stablecoins such as USDT. You should not expect to pay in bitcoin day to day (Bybit 2026).
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, mainly in Yerevan, helped by a large tech sector and many IT workers who moved there since 2022. Events such as Bitcoin Pizza Day gatherings and occasional meetups take place, but not on a big scale (meetup listings; Internet Society 2025).
privacy: Armenia has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Armenia also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.825, ranked 51 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is spending.

name: Aruba
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banking works, but banks have been wary of bitcoin: in 2019 two bitcoin ATMs in Aruba were shut after a bank, RBC, pressured the venues over compliance concerns, though other banks said they had no problem. Expect source-of-funds questions. (CriptoNoticias)
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. Bitcoin is only partly regulated, through the 2024 anti-money-laundering state ordinance, and there is no licensing system (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: Foreigners can move to Aruba, but usually need a job, family ties or proof of solid income or savings. We found no fast investment route aimed at newcomers.
spending: We found no recent news of shops in Aruba accepting bitcoin. The island's only active bitcoin ATM was removed in 2019, so expect to pay in florins or US dollars. (CriptoNoticias)
community: A local group, Bitcoin Aruba, has promoted bitcoin on the island and ran its bitcoin ATM, but we found no regular meetups today. The central bank still warns the public about bitcoin investment schemes, most recently in June 2026. (CriptoNoticias; Centrale Bank van Aruba)
privacy: Aruba has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Aruba also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Australia
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Capital gains are taxed at your normal income tax rate, up to 45%, but the taxable gain is halved for assets held over 12 months (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025; ATO).
banking: Australia's banks are wary of bitcoin, so moving money in and out can be difficult. Commonwealth Bank, the largest, caps payments to bitcoin exchanges at AUD 10,000 a month and can hold or decline transfers for 24 hours, and its subsidiary Bankwest applies similar limits. Bank of Queensland caps bitcoin payments at AUD 5,000 a month, HSBC blocks payments to bitcoin exchanges altogether, Macquarie customers often report declined transfers, and NAB and Westpac block payments to exchanges they consider 'high-risk'. ANZ, ING and several smaller banks are easier to use, but extra fraud checks on larger transfers are common (The Block; Blockworks; Digital Surge banking guide 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The first comprehensive digital asset law was passed in 2026, covering Digital Asset Platforms and Tokenised Custody Platforms under the Corporations Act. Travel Rule obligations, which require platforms to pass on sender and recipient details with transfers, have applied since 1 July 2026 (Contentworks; Elliptic).
residency: Moving here is hard for most people, but there are routes. You need a skilled job, an employer sponsor or family ties. The Skills in Demand visa needs a salary of at least AUD 76,515 in its core stream, and 132,200 of the 185,000 permanent places in 2025–26 are for skilled migrants. The investor visa programme was closed in 2024 and replaced by a National Innovation visa for exceptional talent. (No Borders Law Group 2026; Startup Daily 2024)
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. About 172 merchants are listed (coinpedia).
community: There is an active bitcoin community, with meetups, developers and startups in the major cities. Australia ranked 15th of 117 countries for everyday bitcoin use in Chainalysis's 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index. Attitudes are neutral, with a strong focus on following the rules.
privacy: Limited privacy: bitcoin activity is reported to the tax office and shared with other countries soon. Australia closely tracks bitcoin. Every exchange must register with AUSTRAC, the financial-intelligence agency, and the tax office (ATO) runs a data-matching programme that has requested names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, email and social-media accounts, bank details, wallet addresses and full transaction histories for up to 1.2 million accounts covering July 2023 to June 2026. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, this data is used to check and collect what you owe (ATO via Koinly and Crypto Tax Calculator; OECD June 2026).
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.80, ranked 11 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.602, ranked 20 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for stability. Weakest areas are tax, banking, residency and privacy.

name: Austria
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Bitcoin is taxed at a special rate of 27.5%, the same as dividends and interest (BMF; Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is possible, but you will need a good income or savings. The settlement permit for financially independent people (Niederlassungsbewilligung – ausgenommen Erwerbstätigkeit) needs about EUR 2,548 a month and German language skills, with an annual quota of roughly 450 places (oesterreich.gv.at 2026; Nomad Watch; VigoLex).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. About 131 businesses are listed as accepting it (coinpedia).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events, and Vienna has long been a bitcoin hub. Vienna hosted the bitcoin++ economics edition in May 2026 (bitcoinconferences.info). Austria is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Austria, that is Austria's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.79, ranked 12 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.421, ranked 6 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for stability. Weakest areas are tax and privacy.

name: Azerbaijan
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Local banks are cautious with bitcoin and there are few licensed local exchanges, so most people use peer-to-peer trading or foreign platforms, and banks may question or block related transfers (Central Bank of Azerbaijan).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. Bitcoin is regulated under the Central Bank Regulation on Transactions with Virtual Assets (2023) (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: Short visits are easy with an e-visa, but living here needs a reason: a work permit, family ties, a business, or buying property or investing, which can lead to a temporary residence permit (State Migration Service of Azerbaijan).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin; we found little or no evidence of shops taking it.
community: The bitcoin community is small and mostly focused on trading, with occasional events in Baku but no regular bitcoin meetups we could find.
privacy: Azerbaijan has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2029 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Azerbaijan, that is Azerbaijan's own tax office. Because Azerbaijan taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: the manat has been held at about 1.70 to the US dollar since 2017, after sharp devaluations in 2015. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.142, ranked 109 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax, legal freedom and privacy. Weakest area is spending.

name: Bahamas
tax: The Bahamas has no personal income tax and no capital gains tax, so individuals pay nothing on bitcoin gains.
banking: Around 19 bitcoin businesses are licensed here, but retail bank options are limited: the best-known bitcoin-linked bank says it does not hold or trade bitcoin for clients.
legal: The Bahamas has a modern bitcoin law, updated in 2024, that licenses each type of bitcoin activity. Individuals are free to use bitcoin.
residency: Permanent residency through investment now needs at least $1 million in property or central bank bonds, held for ten years. The threshold was raised from $750,000 in 2025.
spending: Few shops accept bitcoin. The islands' strength is their professional bitcoin industry rather than everyday use.
community: There is a small professional bitcoin community, but we found no grassroots bitcoin events.
privacy: The Bahamas has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the Bahamas, that is the Bahamas's own tax office. Because the Bahamas does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, the reports have little practical effect for residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 51st out of 143 countries, and the Bahamian dollar is tied one-to-one to the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: The Bahamas offers zero tax and a modern bitcoin law, but residency is expensive and everyday bitcoin use is rare.

name: Bahrain
tax: Bahrain has no personal income tax and no capital gains tax, so individuals pay nothing on bitcoin gains.
banking: Rain, Bahrain's licensed bitcoin exchange with more than 2 million customers, lets you top up straight from your bank account. Since May 2026 you can also buy bitcoin through BenefitPay, the national payment app.
legal: Bitcoin is legal and regulated under the Central Bank of Bahrain's dedicated bitcoin rules, among the earliest in the Gulf.
residency: Bahrain's 10-year Golden Residency now needs property worth about $345,000, after the threshold was cut by 35%. It is also open to retirees and professionals.
spending: Paying with bitcoin in everyday shops is still rare. Since 2022 the regulator has allowed the payment firm EazyPay to take bitcoin through Binance Pay at its card terminals and online checkouts (over 5,000 terminals), but the shop receives dinars and we found no reports of this being used much in daily life. (Bitcoin Magazine)
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups in Bahrain. What exists is a business-focused bitcoin and fintech scene, such as Web3 networking evenings in Manama run by exchanges and the Fintech Revolution Summit held in Manama in February 2026. (Luma; Fintech Revolution Summit announcement)
privacy: Bahrain has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. name: Bangladesh
tax: The tax position is harsh here, because bitcoin use is prohibited or cannot be enforced (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Banks are not allowed to deal with bitcoin. Bangladesh Bank says bitcoin deals break the 1947 foreign exchange law and has told banks to watch for and block bitcoin transfers, so people rely on risky peer-to-peer trades. (Bangladesh Bank 2022; Global Law Experts 2026)
legal: Bitcoin is effectively banned. The central bank treats bitcoin transactions as illegal foreign exchange deals, and anonymous trading can also fall under the money laundering law. No law has replaced this stance as of 2026. (Bangladesh Bank 2022; Global Law Experts 2026)
residency: Foreigners usually need a work permit through a local employer, or a Private Investor (PI) visa, which requires a recommendation letter from the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority and an investment in a local business. spending: We found no shops that accept bitcoin. With bitcoin treated as illegal, merchants cannot accept it openly.
community: There is no public bitcoin scene, but use is high underground: Bangladesh ranked 35th of 151 countries in the Chainalysis 2024 adoption index, mostly through peer-to-peer trading. (Chainalysis 2024; The Daily Star 2024)

name: Barbados

Some residents report trouble finding a bank that allows card or transfer payments to bitcoin exchanges, and a local exchange, bitcoin.bb, is one of the few home-grown options. (Expanship 2026; Newhedge)

The Financial Services Commission only published a consultation paper on a framework for bitcoin service providers in April 2026, so for now bitcoin businesses are judged under older financial and securities laws. (Expanship 2026; Newhedge)

These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Barbados, that is Barbados's own tax office. name: Belarus
tax: Since 1 January 2025 bitcoin income falls under the regular Tax Code, but individuals pay no income tax on gains made through licensed High-Tech Park operators such as Bynex or Whitebird, and bitcoin-to-bitcoin swaps and mining are also exempt. Money withdrawn from foreign platforms is taxed at 13%, or 26% if it is not declared. (Myfin.by; Revera Legal)
banking: Several Belarusian banks are under sanctions, and the legal way to swap bitcoin for roubles is through the small set of bitcoin exchanges registered in the High-Tech Park. Since December 2025 access to several offshore exchanges has been blocked, and peer-to-peer trades outside the licensed operators are treated as illegal, so options are narrow. (bne IntelliNews Jan 2026; Myfin.by)
legal: Owning bitcoin is legal, but the state tightly controls how you trade it. A 2024 decree (No. 367) limits buying and selling to Belarusian High-Tech Park exchanges, and a December 2025 decree barred citizens from trading on foreign exchanges, with several offshore sites blocked. A January 2026 decree on state-supervised "bitcoin banks" adds more control, not more freedom for individuals. (ForkLog Sep 2024; bne IntelliNews Jan 2026)
residency: We did not find an easy residence route aimed at foreigners, and the country's political situation and Western sanctions make a move here impractical for most people. (bne IntelliNews Jan 2026)
spending: We found no reports of shops or cafes accepting bitcoin directly; bitcoin is mostly traded through licensed exchanges rather than spent. Treat spending in bitcoin as very limited. (bne IntelliNews Jan 2026; Myfin.by)
community: There is an industry scene around the Minsk High-Tech Park, including the annual Blockchain World summit (third edition held in Minsk on 30 May 2026), but we found no regular grassroots bitcoin meetups. (Onliner May 2026)

name: Belgium
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. From 2026, gains on financial assets are taxed at 10% above a tax-free allowance of EUR 10,000 a year. Speculative or professional trading can still be taxed at 33–50% (Tax Foundation 2026).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is possible, but usually needs a job offer and a good salary. Non-EU workers need a regional work authorisation plus a residence authorisation; the main route for skilled people is the highly qualified worker single permit, which needs a degree, a contract of at least a year and pay of at least the national average gross salary (80% in Flanders for under-30s). Long-term residence becomes possible after 5 years of legal stay (EU Immigration Portal; Belgian Immigration Office).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, and there is little culture of spending it in shops. The number of businesses accepting bitcoin here is modest compared with the leading countries (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, with active meetups and a builder scene connected to the rest of the EU. No major bitcoin conference takes place here, and Belgium is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Belgium, that is Belgium's own tax office. Because Belgium taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

name: Belize

Because Belize taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

name: Bermuda
tax: Bermuda has no personal income tax and no capital gains tax, so individuals pay nothing on bitcoin gains.
banking: Jewel Bank, licensed in 2022, is Bermuda's first digital-asset bank, offering ways to buy and sell bitcoin, storage and bitcoin-backed loans, mainly for businesses. Around 21 licensed bitcoin businesses operate here.
legal: Bermuda has one of the world's most established bitcoin laws, the Digital Asset Business Act, and individuals are free to use bitcoin.
residency: Moving here is expensive: the main residency route needs an investment of at least $2.5 million held for five years, plus 90 days a year on the island.
spending: Few shops accept bitcoin. Bermuda's strength is its professional bitcoin industry rather than everyday use.
community: There is a strong professional bitcoin community for the island's size, although we found no grassroots bitcoin events.
privacy: Bermuda has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Bermuda, that is Bermuda's own tax office. Because Bermuda does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, the reports have little practical effect for residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

name: Bhutan

banking: Local banks are not allowed to help people buy or trade bitcoin. A Royal Monetary Authority notice of 30 April 2025 kept the ban on public bitcoin trading through domestic banks; the only bank link is a licensed digital bank that converts tourist bitcoin payments into local currency for merchants (Lightspark 2025).
legal: Bitcoin is only partly allowed. Since April 2025, bitcoin mining and exchanges are permitted only for companies registered in the Gelephu Mindfulness City special zone, and ordinary residents cannot trade through local banks. The state itself mines and holds bitcoin (Lightspark 2025).
residency: Bhutan is hard to move to, but since January 2026 Gelephu Mindfulness City offers a residence programme for remote professionals and entrepreneurs: about US$2,800 a year plus a refundable US$10,000 deposit, for 12 months renewable once (24 months maximum). Applications are reviewed one by one, and there is no long-term route for most foreigners (Stamped Nomad 2026).

community: The bitcoin scene is small and mostly government-led, through state mining and the Gelephu Mindfulness City. We found no regular grassroots bitcoin meetups (Lightspark 2025; Stamped Nomad 2026).

name: Bolivia, Plurinational State of
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate, but the rules are not yet settled. There is no specific bitcoin tax, so general income tax may apply (Cointelegraph). HelloSafe lists a 15% rate, while TaxAtlas lists 0%.
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. Since the 2024 ban was lifted, state banks now sell the USDT stablecoin (Stablecoin Insider).

Temporary residence is granted for one to three years, with no fixed income threshold: you file a sworn statement of financial means backed by documents such as bank statements, and fees are roughly 280 to 450 US dollars. After three years you can apply for permanent residence. There is no special retiree visa, and practical problems like fuel shortages and roadblocks are worth knowing about. (The Rio Times 2026)

name: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba
tax: The islands have their own Dutch Caribbean tax system, separate from the Netherlands. Residents pay income tax of 30.4% and 35.4% in 2025, with 29.4% and 38.4% proposed for 2026, and profits from substantial shareholdings are taxed at 7.5%. We found no specific rules on bitcoin, so it is unclear how private gains are treated, and regular trading could be taxed as income (Belastingdienst Caribisch Nederland 2025; Rivermate).
banking: The islands use the US dollar, and a handful of local banks in Kralendijk offer normal services, with cards widely accepted. We found no bank that openly serves bitcoin users, so expect a small, conservative banking sector and plan to use foreign exchanges or accounts (Bonaire.com).

community: We found no bitcoin meetups, events or community groups on Bonaire, Sint Eustatius or Saba (Bonaire.com; Armenian Lawyer residency guide 2026).
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the Caribbean Netherlands, that is the Caribbean Netherlands's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: US dollar or Swiss franc or fully dollarised – no local-currency risk. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.

name: Bosnia and Herzegovina

The 2024 anti-money-laundering law requires bitcoin service providers to hold bank accounts and follow strict checks, so expect questions about where your money came from.
