name: Congo
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are not allowed to deal with bitcoin. The regional banking regulator (COBAC) bars banks, microfinance lenders and payment companies in the Central African economic area (CEMAC) from handling bitcoin (Lightspark).
legal: Bitcoin is restricted: you may be able to hold it, but using or trading it is limited. The CEMAC regional banking commission (COBAC) prohibits banks, microfinance institutions and payment companies from handling bitcoin transactions, although owning bitcoin personally is not explicitly outlawed. No bitcoin business licence has been issued under the 2023 COSUMAF regulation (Lightspark; Business in Cameroon 2026).
residency: Moving to the Republic of the Congo realistically needs a job offer: the employer gets a work permit, then you receive a one- to two-year renewable card. Investors in the Pointe-Noire special economic zone need roughly 50 to 100 million CFA francs, and there is no programme for retirees or people living on savings. Paperwork is slow and spread across several offices. (Openshores 2026)
spending: We found no shops in the Republic of the Congo that accept bitcoin. People who use bitcoin rely on person-to-person trades and mobile money. (Newhedge)
community: There is some early interest, such as a conference on bitcoin assets in Brazzaville in October 2025 attended by many students, but we found no regular bitcoin meetups. (AllAfrica 2025)
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Congo, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.40, ranked 123 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.256, ranked 119 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax. Weakest areas are banking and spending.

name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks do not serve bitcoin users: central bank rules require strict anti-money-laundering checks, and bitcoin exchanges and bitcoin payments are not permitted. In the east, banks in Goma and Bukavu have been closed since M23 rebels took those cities in early 2025 (RegAlert 2026; Deutsche Welle, November 2025).
legal: Bitcoin is restricted: you may be able to hold it, but using or trading it is limited under Banque Centrale du Congo Instruction No. 15 (2023) (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: We found no easy residency route for foreigners, and ongoing fighting in the east between the army and M23 rebels makes the Democratic Republic of the Congo a very hard place for most people to settle (Deutsche Welle, November 2025).
spending: We found almost nowhere to spend bitcoin. Accepting bitcoin as payment is not permitted, and reports of bitcoin use in places like Bukavu describe investment apps and schemes rather than paying in shops (RegAlert 2026; Deutsche Welle, November 2025).
community: Some people, for example in Bukavu, have turned to bitcoin apps during the economic crisis, but many have lost money in scams, and we found no regular bitcoin meetups or events (Deutsche Welle, November 2025).
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in DR Congo, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.34, ranked 136 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 3.189, ranked 160 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax. Weakest areas are banking, residency and spending.

name: Cook Islands
tax: The Cook Islands has no capital gains tax, so a private individual selling bitcoin at a profit is generally not taxed. Gains can count as ordinary income (taxed at 0% to 30%) if you trade as a business. There are no bitcoin-specific tax rules. (Expanship 2026; Cook Islands Income Tax Act)
banking: The banking system is small and conservative, and bitcoin-related money flows face extra checks. Most people move funds through New Zealand or Australian banks and exchanges rather than locally. (Expanship 2026)
legal: Holding and using bitcoin is not restricted, but there is no dedicated bitcoin law or licensing regime. Lawmakers have focused on recovering stolen bitcoin, with a Tainted Bitcoin Recovery Bill tabled in 2023 and a ransomware bill under review. (Expanship 2026)
residency: Moving here is hard for most foreigners. Residence is mainly through a job (International Worker Permit), family ties or an approved resident-investor permit, and permanent residence is tightly limited. (Cook Islands Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Immigration; VisaAtlas 2026)
spending: We found no shops that accept bitcoin, so there is effectively nowhere to spend it.
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups or visible local bitcoin groups. (Meetup listings)
privacy: The Cook Islands has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. The Cook Islands also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Costa Rica
tax: Costa Rica has no law aimed specifically at bitcoin tax. Depending on your situation, gains may be treated as ordinary income or taxed at 15% as capital gains. Income earned abroad is generally not taxed.
banking: Banks accept money linked to bitcoin if you provide paperwork, but they are conservative and some cautious behaviour is common.
legal: Bitcoin is legal and unrestricted, with no dedicated law limiting what individuals can do.
residency: Costa Rica's long-standing routes for retirees, people with passive income and investors are well established and popular with people moving from abroad.
spending: Bitcoin Jungle, around Dominical and Uvita, is one of the region's best examples of a working bitcoin economy, with many local businesses accepting payments over the Lightning Network.
community: Costa Rica has one of Latin America's strongest grassroots bitcoin communities, focused on education and everyday payments.
privacy: Costa Rica has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Costa Rica, that is Costa Rica's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Costa Rica's rule of law 28th out of 143 countries, second best in Latin America. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 61st of 163 countries.
summary: Costa Rica is a favourite with bitcoiners for its strong grassroots community, real bitcoin economies and stable democracy. Tax rules are less clear-cut than in the top-ranked countries.

name: Croatia
tax: Croatia does not tax gains on bitcoin held for more than two years. Gains on bitcoin held for a shorter time are taxed at an effective rate of about 12%.
banking: Like the rest of the EU, residents can use banks such as Revolut, N26 and bunq that sell bitcoin inside their apps, and send money to licensed exchanges by ordinary bank transfer. Local banks vary in how welcoming they are, and large transfers may be checked.
legal: The EU's bitcoin rules have applied fully since the end of 2024. Individuals are free to hold, store in their own wallets and trade bitcoin, although platforms must record details of transfers to and from personal wallets.
residency: Croatia's digital nomad residence needs an income of about €2,540 a month, and income earned abroad is not taxed during the stay.
spending: Some businesses in Zagreb and along the coast accept bitcoin, but the number is modest compared with the leading countries.
community: There are active bitcoin meetups and start-ups, although no major bitcoin conference takes place here.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Croatia, that is Croatia's own tax office. Because Croatia taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Croatia uses the euro, and the World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 46th out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 23rd of 163 countries.
summary: Croatia is an attractive EU option for patient holders, with no tax after two years, an accessible nomad visa and the stability of the euro.

name: Cuba
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks offer no route to bitcoin. Because of the US embargo, Cubans cannot sign up for big exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken or Binance, so bitcoin is bought and sold almost entirely person to person through Telegram and WhatsApp groups, paid in pesos or mobile transfers. (Cointelegraph 2023; CriptoNoticias 2026)
legal: The Central Bank of Cuba recognised virtual assets in 2021 (Resolution 215), but use needs its authorisation. In March 2026 Resolution 4/2026 licensed about ten businesses to use bitcoin for cross-border payments through approved providers only, with quarterly reporting. This does not open things up for ordinary people, and self-custody wallets are not part of the scheme. (Cubanet 2026; CriptoNoticias 2026)
residency: Moving here is hard for most foreigners. A new immigration law announced in May 2026 broadens the grounds for permanent residence to include family ties, time spent in the country, professional skills and investment, but no clear investor amounts or procedures have been published yet. (Telemundo 2026)
spending: A small group of private businesses in Havana accept bitcoin, mostly over the Lightning Network; more than ten were reported in 2023, including bars and restaurants. Use is informal and limited to a few spots. (Cointelegraph 2023)
community: Cuba has a lively grassroots community. The Cuba Bitcoin group runs education events and meetups in Havana (over 60 people at one), local developers have built their own Lightning wallets and a person-to-person trading node, and remittance service BitRemesas has tens of thousands of users. (Cointelegraph 2023; CriptoNoticias 2026)
privacy: Cuba closely monitors financial activity or limits money leaving the country, and bitcoin use is watched or restricted by the authorities.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: the peso hit a record 500 per US dollar on the informal market in 2026, against official rates as low as 24, and an average state salary is worth about 14 US dollars. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.139, ranked 108 of 163 countries. (El Toque via AOL 2026)
summary: Best for tax and community. Weakest areas are banking and privacy.

name: Curaçao
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banking works but is compliance-heavy. In 2025 the central bank warned that without a proper bitcoin law Curaçao risked FATF grey-listing and 'financial isolation', and local fintech groups say regulation is needed to open doors to banks. (Curaçao Chronicle, February 2025)
legal: Owning bitcoin is legal, but the rules are still being built. Since July 2024 bitcoin firms must register with the Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten, and a full licensing law for bitcoin service providers was proposed in late 2024 but was not yet in force in 2025. (Curaçao Chronicle, 2024–2025)
residency: Curaçao has an investor permit: about US$280,000 for a 3-year permit, US$425,000 for 5 years, or US$850,000 for an indefinite permit. There is also a route for retirees and people living on their own income, without needing a job offer. (IMI Daily; VisaAtlas 2026)
spending: We found no news reports of shops in Curaçao accepting bitcoin, so paying with it in daily life appears rare.
community: There is a small but real scene: Bitkaya in Willemstad hosts small in-person bitcoin roundtables (for example in July 2025), and the island has a fintech association. We found no large regular meetups. (Bitkaya; Curaçao Chronicle)
privacy: Curaçao has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Curaçao also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is spending.

name: Cyprus
tax: Since 1 January 2026, Cyprus taxes profits from selling bitcoin at a flat 8%, one of the lowest rates in the EU.
banking: Like the rest of the EU, residents can use banks such as Revolut, N26 and bunq that sell bitcoin inside their apps, and send money to licensed exchanges by ordinary bank transfer. Local banks vary in how welcoming they are, and large transfers may be checked.
legal: The EU's bitcoin rules have applied fully since the end of 2024. Individuals are free to hold, store in their own wallets and trade bitcoin, although platforms must record details of transfers to and from personal wallets.
residency: Cyprus offers residence for people with a pension or passive income from about $861 a month, and a digital nomad visa for those earning about €3,500 a month.
spending: Some businesses in tech and tourism areas accept bitcoin, but the number is modest compared with the leading countries.
community: Cyprus has a strong bitcoin and financial-services industry, although no major bitcoin conference takes place here.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Cyprus, that is Cyprus's own tax office. Because Cyprus taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Cyprus uses the euro, and the World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 30th out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 79th of 163 countries.
summary: Cyprus combines a low 8% bitcoin tax, affordable residency and EU stability.

name: Czechia
tax: Since 2025, Czechia does not tax gains on bitcoin held for more than three years, or yearly bitcoin income below CZK 100,000. Other gains are taxed at 15%, or 23% for higher earners.
banking: Czechia uses the standard EU banking system, though some banks remain cautious with money linked to bitcoin.
legal: The EU's bitcoin rules apply, and individuals are free to hold and use bitcoin.
residency: Residency follows the usual EU routes, through work, a business or family.
spending: Prague has one of Europe's strongest bitcoin shopping cultures, and Alza, the country's largest electronics retailer, has accepted bitcoin since 2017.
community: Czechia has a deep bitcoin culture. Prague hosts BTC Prague, Europe's largest bitcoin-only conference, and the country is home to the famous Paralelní Polis community space.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Czechia, that is Czechia's own tax office. Because Czechia taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Czechia's rule of law 20th out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 13th of 163 countries.
summary: Czechia is one of Europe's real bitcoin capitals, with a famous community, plenty of places to spend bitcoin and tax-free gains after three years.

name: Côte d'Ivoire
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks in the West African currency union are conservative and do not offer bitcoin services, and the regional central bank (BCEAO) has repeatedly warned about bitcoin. Most people buy and sell bitcoin person-to-person, often paying through mobile money such as Orange Money, MTN or Wave, rather than through a bank account (BCEAO; Ecofin Agency 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. The regional central bank (BCEAO) has never banned people from holding or using bitcoin, but there are no rules for it yet. A drafting committee (C-CRYPTO) was set up in 2026, with no timeline (Ecofin Agency Jul 2026; Kolonell Jun 2026).
residency: Citizens of West African (ECOWAS) countries can live and work here freely. Other foreigners get a residence card through a job, family ties or by setting up a business, which can be registered fairly quickly through the investment promotion centre (CEPICI). There is no special nomad or passive-income visa (CEPICI; Côte d'Ivoire immigration rules).
spending: Almost nowhere accepts bitcoin. Everyday payments run on cash and mobile money, and we found no meaningful cluster of shops taking bitcoin in Abidjan or elsewhere.
community: There is a small bitcoin scene in Abidjan, with occasional events such as exchange-run education meetups, Stellar meetups and bitcoin conventions, but no well-established regular bitcoin meetup (Digital Mag CI 2025; Luma).
privacy: Côte d'Ivoire has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Côte d'Ivoire also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.44, ranked 106 of 143 countries. Currency: the West African CFA franc has a fixed peg to the euro, though it was devalued in 1994 and its reform is debated. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: a regional bitcoin framework is being drafted with no set timeline. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.061, ranked 92 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is spending.

name: Denmark
tax: Bitcoin is heavily taxed here, or the tax rules are harsh. Most bitcoin gains are treated as speculative income and taxed at more than 50% at the top rate (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: EU citizens can move freely, but for others Denmark is hard. The main fast-track work permit needs a salary of at least 552,000 kroner a year in 2026, other routes need a shortage-list job or an approved start-up, and family reunification rules are strict. There is no retiree or digital nomad visa, and permanent residence normally takes eight years. (Revolut 2026; Commoner Law 2026)
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, and there is little culture of spending it in shops. The number of businesses accepting bitcoin here is modest compared with the leading countries (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community of tech-savvy people, rather than everyday users. No major bitcoin conference takes place here, and it is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Denmark, that is Denmark's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.90, ranked 1 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.504, ranked 11 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for stability. Weakest area is tax.

name: Djibouti
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Djibouti has 13 licensed banks, which are described as very risk-averse. None has published a policy on bitcoin, bitcoin-related clients can expect extra checks, and we found no bitcoin exchange based in the country, so most people would rely on peer-to-peer trades or foreign accounts (Blockspot Djibouti profile; RegAlert crypto guide 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. Bitcoin companies are licensed under Central Bank Circular No. 2025-01 (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: There is no digital nomad or retirement visa. Foreigners usually get a residence card (carte de séjour) through a job with a local employer and a work permit, or through family ties or a significant investment, and permanent residence is only possible after many years, case by case (Rivermate Djibouti guide).
spending: We found no shops, ATMs or businesses known to accept bitcoin in Djibouti, so in practice you cannot spend it locally (Blockspot Djibouti profile).
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups, local groups or bitcoin businesses, so there is no visible bitcoin community (Blockspot Djibouti profile).
privacy: Djibouti has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Djibouti also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.098, ranked 104 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Dominica
tax: You pay no tax on bitcoin gains here as a private individual. Dominica has no capital gains, wealth or inheritance tax. Income tax applies to income such as wages or business profits: the first EC$30,000 a year is tax-free, then rates of 15%, 25% and 35% apply, so trading bitcoin as a business could be taxed as income (Dominica Inland Revenue Division; Dominica Citizenship by Investment Unit).
banking: Banks are wary of bitcoin, so moving money in and out can be difficult. The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank urges the public to treat bitcoin as high-risk, we found no bank in the region publicly offering bitcoin services, and regional banks are under pressure from international partner banks to avoid risky clients (ECCB via Caribbean Today; Euronews).
legal: Bitcoin is legal, and individuals are free to use it, but bitcoin businesses need a licence. Dominica passed the Virtual Asset Business Act in 2022 and follow-up regulations in 2024, supervised by the Financial Services Unit, which only allows listed, authorised firms to operate (Dominica Financial Services Unit).
residency: Moving here is easy and affordable for most people. Citizenship by investment starts from $200,000 (Henley & Partners).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, and we found no merchant data or recent activity on BTC Map. The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank discourages the use of bitcoin (BTC Map blog; Eastern Caribbean Central Bank).
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, mostly made up of small bitcoin-aware groups. We found no bitcoin conference or circular-economy project planned for 2026, including in the Federation of Bitcoin Circular Economies material.
privacy: Dominica has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Dominica also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.58, ranked 54 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for tax, residency and privacy. Weakest areas are banking, spending and community.

name: Dominican Republic
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: The Central Bank says bitcoin is not legal tender, and regulated banks are not allowed to deal in bitcoin themselves. There is still no licensing system for exchanges (two bills were in Congress in 2026). People use bank transfers from banks like Banreservas or Banco Popular to fund P2P trades, plus bitcoin ATMs, but banks will not handle bitcoin directly. (Kryptonim 2026; DPL News)
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. There is no formal regulatory framework, and the central bank says the peso is the only legal tender (rankingslatam).
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. Under Law 171-07, the pensioner (pensionado) residence needs at least US$1,500 a month and the rentista residence at least US$2,000 a month, and qualifying income is exempt from local income tax. You can become eligible for citizenship after 2 years (MigratioLex; Rio Times Sep 2026).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. In Santo Domingo, the local community counts more than 100 businesses accepting bitcoin, and Samaná has its own bitcoin circular economy (CriptoNoticias).
community: The Dominican Republic has a fast-growing bitcoin community. The group Satoshi Somos Todos helped grow the number of shops accepting bitcoin from 65 to 115 in three months in 2025, working in Santo Domingo, Samaná, Punta Cana and Monte Cristi, and Bitcoin Dominicana runs meetups in Santo Domingo's Colonial Zone. (CriptoNoticias 2025; Luma)
privacy: The Dominican Republic has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. The Dominican Republic also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.50, ranked 76 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.038, ranked 88 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is banking.

name: Ecuador
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: People can buy bitcoin with cash, cards or local bank transfers, and since 2025 there are bitcoin ATMs in Quito and Cuenca. But there are no rules for bitcoin firms yet, and the central bank says bitcoin is not supervised by any Ecuadorian body, so banks may ask questions about bitcoin money. (Primicias 2024 and 2025)
legal: Bitcoin is restricted. It is legal to hold and trade, but paying with bitcoin is banned (Art. 98, Monetary Code) and banks block bitcoin transactions (Wikipedia).
residency: Moving here is easy and affordable for most people. The digital nomad visa requires from about $1,380 a month (globalcitizensolutions).
spending: Bitcoin is not an allowed means of payment: in August 2024 the central bank said it will report businesses that take bitcoin as payment to the prosecutor's office. We found no recent reports of shops accepting it. (Primicias 2024)
community: The community is small. There are bitcoin ATMs in Quito and Cuenca and some grassroots education, such as bitcoin workshops in Quito schools, but we found no regular bitcoin meetups. (CriptoNoticias 2023; Primicias 2025)
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Ecuador, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.46, ranked 99 of 143 countries. Currency: US dollar or Swiss franc or fully dollarised – no local-currency risk. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.539, ranked 134 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for residency. Weakest area is spending.

name: Egypt
tax: Egypt has no specific tax on bitcoin, and personal gains are not clearly taxed. But dealing in bitcoin without a central bank licence is illegal and no one holds a licence, so you cannot legally benefit from this (TaxAtlas 2026; Central Bank of Egypt).
banking: Banks follow the Central Bank of Egypt's ban on bitcoin dealings and block card payments and transfers to bitcoin exchanges. No bitcoin platform has been licensed, so people rely on informal person-to-person trades, with a real risk of frozen accounts. (Central Bank of Egypt; Banking Law 194 of 2020; Waltio 2026)
legal: Bitcoin is banned or very heavily restricted. Individuals, banks and financial institutions may not deal in bitcoin without a licence (Wikipedia).
residency: Egypt is fairly easy to move to if you have savings. A US$50,000 deposit at the National Bank of Egypt is marketed as giving a one-year renewable residence permit, and US$100,000 a three-year one. Buying property also qualifies: at least US$100,000 for a three-year permit and US$200,000 for five years. (IMI Daily 2026)
spending: Because trading and promoting bitcoin without a central bank licence is illegal, shops do not openly accept bitcoin. We found almost no merchants. (Central Bank of Egypt)
community: Many Egyptians use bitcoin quietly through person-to-person apps, but the legal ban and a religious ruling against bitcoin by Dar al-Ifta keep the community low-key, with few public meetups. (Waltio 2026; Dar al-Ifta)
privacy: Bitcoin is banned or very heavily restricted in Egypt, so any bitcoin activity carries legal risk and is closely watched.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.35, ranked 135 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.186, ranked 112 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for residency. Weakest areas are tax, banking, legal freedom, spending and privacy.

name: El Salvador
tax: El Salvador does not tax gains on bitcoin, and a 2024 reform confirmed that income earned abroad is tax-free for residents and non-residents alike. There is no wealth, inheritance or gift tax. Unusually, the bitcoin exemption is written directly into law.
banking: Bitcoin wallets, exchanges and payment apps operate freely, and the government launched its own Chivo wallet in 2021. Local banks, however, are still cautious about money linked to bitcoin, Chivo use has fallen, and some bitcoin businesses bank in neighbouring Panama instead.
legal: El Salvador has the most bitcoin-specific laws in the world, including the 2021 Bitcoin Law and a 2023 law allowing bitcoin-backed bonds. Since January 2025, under an agreement with the IMF, businesses are no longer required to accept bitcoin, but holding, using and paying with it remains completely legal.
residency: Temporary residency is available through modest investment and other routes. The Freedom Visa offers citizenship within weeks for a $1 million investment in bitcoin or USDT, limited to 1,000 people a year. A Salvadoran passport gives visa-free travel to around 130 countries.

banking: Local advisers report that Georgia's two largest banks, Bank of Georgia and TBC, generally work with clients who receive money from bitcoin. Over-the-counter trading desks and bitcoin ATMs are common in Tbilisi and Batumi. Normal source-of-funds checks apply.
legal: Bitcoin is fully legal for individuals. Since 2023, bitcoin businesses have needed a licence from the National Bank of Georgia, which also banned licensed firms from lending bitcoin to individuals.
residency: Citizens of around 95 countries can live in Georgia for up to a year without a visa. Residence permits are available through buying property, owning a business or working, with comparatively low thresholds.
spending: You can pay in bitcoin at a visible cluster of cafés, co-working spaces and services in Tbilisi and Batumi, and bitcoin ATMs are widespread. Acceptance is not yet nationwide.
community: Cheap hydropower turned Georgia into a bitcoin-mining hub. It also has an active meetup and trading culture and a sizeable community of bitcoin entrepreneurs who have moved there.
privacy: Georgia has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Georgia also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Georgia's rule of law 52nd out of 143 countries. The local currency, the lari, can lose value, and the country has been in a political crisis since 2024, though there have been no moves against bitcoin. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 93rd of 163 countries.
summary: Georgia combines no tax on bitcoin profits, a year of visa-free living for many nationalities and strong privacy. The main risks are a volatile currency and political uncertainty.

name: Germany
tax: In Germany, bitcoin held privately for more than a year can be sold tax-free. Gains on bitcoin held for less than a year, above a small annual allowance, are taxed as income at up to more than 40%. A government draft would replace the one-year rule with a 25% flat tax from 2027, but this is not yet law.
banking: Germany has a deep, closely supervised bitcoin market, and mainstream banks and savings banks are adding bitcoin trading and storage for everyday customers.
legal: The EU's bitcoin rules and Germany's financial regulator apply. Individuals are free to hold, store and spend bitcoin.
residency: For people from outside the EU, residency usually requires a job, a place to study or family ties, and the paperwork can be heavy.
spending: Berlin and other cities have bitcoin-accepting businesses, and Germany is among the leading countries for listed merchants, but paying in bitcoin is not yet mainstream.
community: Germany has a strong bitcoin community of developers, meetups and long-time enthusiasts.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Germany, that is Germany's own tax office. Because Germany taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Germany has excellent rule of law, uses the euro and has strong institutions. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 28th of 163 countries.
summary: Germany is one of the best places for long-term bitcoin holders, thanks to tax-free gains after a year, mainstream bank access and a strong community. Watch for the proposed tax change in 2027.

name: Ghana
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks remain cautious. Even after the new bitcoin law, the Bank of Ghana ordered all banks, payment companies and mobile-money issuers in June 2026 to cut ties with bitcoin platforms offering unauthorised dollar wallets to Ghanaians. Licensing of bitcoin firms is being rolled out in phases during 2026, so many people still rely on person-to-person trading (Bank of Ghana via News Ghana; US International Trade Administration).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The Virtual Asset Service Providers Act 2025 (Act 1154) is in force, and the SEC and the Bank of Ghana are setting up licensing and a testing scheme for new firms during 2026 (finhive.africa; compliance7).
residency: Living in Ghana for more than 180 days needs a residence permit, and working needs a separate work permit sponsored by a registered Ghanaian company. Permits last one year and cost about US$1,000 for non-West Africans, plus medical and ID card fees. There is no retirement or digital nomad route, so most people need a job or their own registered business (Mondaq 2025 guide).
spending: Bitcoin is mostly traded and used for transfers rather than spent in shops. We found no evidence of a cluster of shops where you can regularly pay with bitcoin (US International Trade Administration; News Ghana).
community: There is a small but real community. BitDevs Accra holds meetups at the University of Ghana (54 people attended in June 2026), and the Built With Bitcoin Foundation runs a Bitcoin Technology Center in Ejisu offering free classes and meetups (Luma; Nasdaq).
privacy: Ghana has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Ghana also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.54, ranked 63 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.943, ranked 75 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are banking, residency and spending.

name: Gibraltar
tax: Private individuals in Gibraltar pay no tax on capital gains from personal assets, including bitcoin.
banking: Xapo Bank is both a fully licensed bank and a licensed bitcoin business in Gibraltar, offering bitcoin and regular accounts in one place. Local banks are used to working with licensed bitcoin firms.
legal: Gibraltar created the world's first purpose-built licensing system for bitcoin businesses in 2018 and updated it in 2025. Individuals are completely free to use bitcoin.
residency: Residency is hard to get unless you have a job or a business there, or are wealthy. The special Category 2 status for wealthy newcomers now needs net assets of at least GBP 5 million (up from GBP 2 million for applications before June 2026), plus approved housing in Gibraltar and a minimum yearly tax of GBP 37,000. (PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries)
spending: A handful of Main Street shops have taken bitcoin. In 2022 the franchise group Sandpiper enabled Lightning payments in seven stores, including Costa Coffee, Hotel Chocolat, Card Factory and The Gibraltar Bakery, using CoinCorner's tap-to-pay Bolt Card. In 2021 the Essardas group said its seven jewellery shops would accept bitcoin. These reports are a few years old, so check before you rely on them. (Benzinga 2022; Gibraltar Chronicle 2021)
community: Gibraltar has a sizeable licensed bitcoin industry, and its government promotes it at conferences abroad such as Consensus Hong Kong 2026 and the GIBLDN25 DLT Forum in London. But we found no regular grassroots bitcoin meetups on the Rock itself, so the community you can join day to day is small and mostly professional. (HM Government of Gibraltar 2026; Gibraltar Chronicle 2025)
privacy: Gibraltar has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Gibraltar, that is Gibraltar's own tax office. Because Gibraltar taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Gibraltar is very stable, its pound is tied to sterling, and its bitcoin rules have been consistent since 2018. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Gibraltar combines tax-free gains, an actual bitcoin bank and the world's longest-running bitcoin licensing system. Getting residency is the main challenge, and the grassroots bitcoin community is small.

name: Greece
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate. Under the 2025/2026 tax code update, bitcoin capital gains are taxed at a flat 15% (Waltio guide 2026).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is possible, but you will need a good income or savings. The digital nomad visa requires €3,500 a month (destivity).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in Athens and tourist areas. It is a niche, but it works. The number of businesses accepting bitcoin here is modest compared with the leading countries (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, with active bitcoin meetups and many everyday investors. No major bitcoin conference takes place here, and the country is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Greece, that is Greece's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.60, ranked 48 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.828, ranked 53 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for banking, legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are tax, residency, spending, community and privacy.

name: Greenland
tax: Bitcoin tax here is unclear. Greenland has its own tax system, separate from Denmark's, and as a main rule private individuals do not pay tax on capital gains; but gains on assets bought as a business or for speculation are taxed as ordinary income at about 36% to 44%, and there is no official guidance on bitcoin (PwC Greenland tax summary; Greenland income tax bill EM2025/13).
banking: Banking is workable but cautious. Greenland's main banks, such as Grønlandsbanken and BankNordik, follow Danish anti-money-laundering rules, so transfers to and from European exchanges usually work but you should expect source-of-funds questions (Danish Financial Supervisory Authority; Grønlandsbanken).
legal: Individuals are free to buy, hold and self-custody bitcoin. Financial services are supervised by the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority, and because Greenland is outside the EU, Europe's MiCA bitcoin rules do not automatically apply and there are no local licensed bitcoin firms (Danish FSA; PwC).
residency: Moving here usually needs a job. Nordic citizens can live and work freely, while everyone else needs a residence and work permit for Greenland, normally based on a job offer, family ties or study; there is no investment or digital nomad visa (Danish immigration service, rules for Greenland).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. We found no shops in Greenland and no businesses advertising bitcoin payments.
community: There is no visible bitcoin community. We found no bitcoin meetups or groups; the bitcoin talk about Greenland is mostly outside speculation about mining with its hydropower (CryptoSlate).
privacy: Greenland has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2027 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Greenland, that is Greenland's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Mostly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the Danish krone, which is pegged to the euro. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: Danish-style financial regulation, with no sign of a bitcoin crackdown. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Grenada
tax: Grenada has no capital gains tax, so personal bitcoin gains are not taxed unless they amount to business income.
banking: Banking is the weak spot. The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank urges people to treat bitcoin as high-risk, we found no local bank openly offering bitcoin services, and Caribbean banks are under pressure from international partner banks to avoid risky clients.
legal: Grenada has adopted the regional bitcoin law drafted by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank. Individuals are free to use bitcoin.
residency: Grenada offers citizenship by investment from about $235,000. Its passport is popular because Grenada has a treaty with the US that allows its citizens to apply for an investor visa.
spending: We found no recent data on businesses accepting bitcoin, and the regional central bank discourages using bitcoin for payments.
community: There are only small bitcoin-aware circles, with no major community or events.
privacy: Grenada has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Grenada also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Grenada's rule of law 49th out of 143 countries, and the Eastern Caribbean dollar is firmly tied to the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Grenada offers zero tax on personal gains, an affordable citizenship programme and good privacy. Banking and everyday bitcoin use remain limited.

name: Guadeloupe
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Guadeloupe is a French overseas department, so French tax law applies: gains are taxed only once your yearly bitcoin sales exceed €305, and then at the flat tax, which rose from 30% to 31.4% after the 2026 social security budget raised the CSG levy from 9.2% to 10.6% (MoneyVox 2026).
banking: Banking works, but some banks are cautious and transfers may be checked. Guadeloupe uses the euro and the French banking system, and since 1 July 2026 only providers authorised by France's financial markets authority (AMF) under the EU's MiCA rules may serve French clients (83 of 117 French providers were authorised by mid-May 2026). French banks still sometimes question or block transfers to bitcoin platforms, or close accounts as an anti-money-laundering precaution, so using an authorised platform and keeping records helps. In 2024 the overseas branch of the Banque de France (IEDOM) publicly warned overseas investors about bitcoin risks. (Actu-Juridique Sep 2026; Cryptoactu Jun 2026; RCI)
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Residency follows French law, so EU citizens can move here freely. Everyone else needs a French long-stay visa or residence permit through the usual French routes such as work, family or study. Note that Guadeloupe is outside the Schengen area: a Schengen visa does not cover it, and short visits need a separate overseas visa unless you are exempt (French Ministry of the Interior).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, if any. We found no news reports of local shops in Guadeloupe taking bitcoin, so day-to-day life runs on euros by card and cash, and bitcoin spending is mostly limited to online services (our search of local and French news, October 2026).
community: There is very little visible bitcoin community. We found no regular bitcoin meetups or events in Pointe-à-Pitre or Basse-Terre; local bitcoiners mostly connect through the wider French community online (our search of local and French news, October 2026).
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Guadeloupe, that is Guadeloupe's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the euro. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: EU-wide MiCA rules give a stable framework, though French tax on gains has changed, most recently in 2026. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are tax, spending, community and privacy.

name: Guam
tax: Guam uses a 'mirror' of the US tax code, so bitcoin is taxed as property: long-term gains at 0%, 15% or 20% and short-term gains at ordinary income rates. Residents file with Guam's Department of Revenue and Taxation instead of the IRS, and every bitcoin sale must be reported (Taxes for Expats Guam guide 2026; IRS).
banking: Banking follows US rules and US payment channels, so documented users can generally move money to and from regulated US exchanges. Compliance checks are as strict as on the mainland, and Guam has no bitcoin rules of its own (Freeman Law; IRS).
legal: Individuals can freely hold, self-custody, spend and trade bitcoin, which the IRS treats as property. Guam has not passed its own bitcoin law, so federal US rules for bitcoin businesses apply (IRS; Freeman Law).
residency: US citizens can move here freely, but US visa rules apply to Guam. The Guam–Northern Mariana Islands visa waiver only allows visits of up to 45 days for nationals of 12 countries, so everyone else needs regular US immigration status such as a work visa or green card (Wikipedia: Visa policy of the United States).
spending: Guam had an early burst of interest around 2017–2018, when local advocates counted dozens of businesses accepting bitcoin and a first bitcoin ATM opened at a coffee shop. We found no recent reports confirming how many still accept it, so you should not count on spending bitcoin day to day (Pacific Island Times, 2018).
community: Guam had a visible group of bitcoin enthusiasts around 2017–2018, but we found no current regular meetups or events. Today the community appears small and informal (Pacific Island Times, 2018).
privacy: US federal rules apply here, so bitcoin brokers report trades to the US tax office (IRS). These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Guam, that is Guam's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: US dollar or Swiss franc or fully dollarised – no local-currency risk. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for banking, legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are tax, residency, spending, community and privacy.

name: Guatemala
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate, but the treatment is not yet settled. TaxAtlas lists 0% because there is no specific bitcoin rule, while Cointelegraph reports capital gains tax of up to 15%. ECIJA 2025 notes that bitcoin is not expressly recognised in tax law.
banking: Banking works, but some banks are cautious and transfers may be checked or delayed. Banco Industrial works with SukuPay so people can receive money from abroad in the USDC stablecoin (riotimesonline).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and individuals are free to use it, with no restrictive rules. Use is growing naturally, and Banco Industrial offers USDC stablecoin remittances through SukuPay (Rankings Latam; Rio Times Online).
residency: Moving here is easy and affordable for most people. Rentista or pensionado residency is available from US$1,250 a month, plus US$300 for each dependant, and it is granted as permanent residency from day one (IGM Acuerdo IGM-016-2025; Rio Times 2026).
spending: Bitcoin spending is concentrated around Lake Atitlán. The Bitcoin Lake project in Panajachel has signed up around 60–70 local businesses since 2022, including cafés, hotels and tuk-tuk drivers, and San Marcos has a few merchants and a bitcoin ATM. Outside the lake area, acceptance is rare. (Bitcoin News 2023; Bitcoin Beach 2025; Bloomberg Línea 2022)
community: There is a small but real grassroots community, centred on Bitcoin Lake in Panajachel. It teaches bitcoin in local schools and Mayan communities, and its gatherings have grown to dozens of people. We found little sign of regular meetups in Guatemala City. (Bitcoin Beach 2025; CriptoNoticias 2023)
privacy: Guatemala has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Bitcoin gains are still taxed, so you need to declare them yourself.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.44, ranked 110 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.025, ranked 87 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for residency. Weakest areas are tax, banking, spending, community and stability.

name: Guernsey
tax: Guernsey has no capital gains tax, so selling bitcoin you hold as a personal investment is not taxed. Only bitcoin that counts as income, such as frequent trading as a business, mining or staking rewards, falls under the flat 20% income tax. Bitcoin platforms report to the tax office under the new international reporting rules from 2026. (PwC Tax Summaries; Walkers 2026)
banking: Banks here are mostly branches of big UK banks, which are careful with bitcoin and ask detailed source-of-funds questions. The island's banking sector is small and not known for serving bitcoin firms, so many people also use UK or European payment providers. (Expanship 2026)
legal: Individuals can hold, trade and self-custody bitcoin freely. Bitcoin businesses need a licence from the Guernsey Financial Services Commission under the Lending, Credit and Finance Law 2022, and licensed firms may only serve professional, not retail, clients. (Guernsey FSC; Expanship 2026)
residency: British and Irish citizens can move freely, but others need a UK-style visa such as a work permit. Most homes are on the local housing market, which needs a job-linked permit, so outsiders usually buy or rent on the much pricier Open Market. (States of Guernsey)
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin. Guernsey's bitcoin activity is mostly in the finance industry, not in shops.
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, mostly made up of finance and tech professionals, with occasional events rather than a busy meetup scene.
privacy: Guernsey has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2027 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Guernsey, that is Guernsey's own tax office. Because Guernsey does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, the reports have little practical effect for residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for tax and stability. Weakest areas are residency and spending.

name: Guinea
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks do not offer bitcoin services. In August 2026 the central bank said it has authorised no one to trade or invest in bitcoin, and told mobile money and payment firms such as Orange Money to find, block and report accounts used for bitcoin fraud (Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea via Droit Médias Finance).
legal: Holding bitcoin is not banned, but it has no legal status. In an August 2026 notice the central bank said bitcoin is not legal tender, is not regulated or guaranteed by any authority, and that unlicensed firms collecting money for bitcoin is acting illegally (Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea via Droit Médias Finance).
residency: You can live here with a job or a business. Employees need a work permit from the Ministry of Labour and then a renewable one-year residence card, while investors need a registered company and proof of capital. People without local work or a sponsor find it difficult (Open Shores).
spending: We found no shops that accept bitcoin and no news of merchants taking it.
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups or visible local bitcoin groups.
privacy: Guinea has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Guinea also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.41, ranked 117 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.220, ranked 115 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are banking, spending and community.

name: Guinea-Bissau
tax: Guinea-Bissau has no specific rules for bitcoin. Personal income tax could apply to gains, but the tax office has not said how it treats bitcoin, so the position is unclear (Blockspot 2026).
banking: Banking for bitcoin users is hard. The banking sector is small, no bank has a formal policy for bitcoin customers, and mobile money is the main digital payment channel, so most people buy and sell through person-to-person trades or international platforms. Regional foreign-exchange rules adopted by the BCEAO in late 2024 also limit cross-border money flows (Blockspot 2026; Newhedge 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. The regional central bank (BCEAO) has never banned people from holding or using bitcoin, but there are no rules for it yet. A drafting committee (C-CRYPTO) was set up in 2026, with no timeline (Ecofin Agency Jul 2026; Kolonell Jun 2026).
residency: Moving here is difficult for most foreigners. There is no special visa for remote workers, retirees or investors, and the country's small economy and institutions make settling in slow and uncertain (Blockspot 2026).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. We found no shops or businesses taking bitcoin, and no local bitcoin exchanges, wallets or companies are listed for the country (Blockspot 2026; Newhedge 2026).
community: There is no visible bitcoin community. We found no regular bitcoin meetups or events, and the little use that exists happens informally through person-to-person transfers (Blockspot 2026).
privacy: Guinea-Bissau has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Bitcoin gains are still taxed, so you need to declare them yourself.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: the West African CFA franc, fixed to the euro at 655.957 francs per euro. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: a regional bitcoin framework is being drafted for the eight-country WAEMU union. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.012, ranked 84 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Guyana
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: There are no licensed bitcoin trading platforms in Guyana, and the government says it has no plans yet to facilitate bitcoin transactions through the financial system. In practice people buy and sell bitcoin person to person or through foreign platforms (Sigma; CBC Barbados 2025).
legal: Holding bitcoin is not banned, but bitcoin is not legal tender and there is no bitcoin law. The central bank has warned the public several times about the risks, and in February 2025 Vice President Bharrat Jagdeo said Guyana has no immediate plans to regulate bitcoin until wider financial reforms are done (CBC Barbados; Sigma).
residency: There is no retirement or digital nomad visa. Foreigners who want to work need a work permit from the Ministry of Home Affairs, which lasts for the length of the job contract (up to three years), and residence permits are usually granted for one year at a time, renewable (PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries 2026).
spending: We found no evidence of shops in Guyana accepting bitcoin. Bitcoin use is described as limited, with bitcoin payments for everyday goods still only a future possibility (Sigma).
community: The bitcoin community is small. We found no regular public bitcoin meetups, and bitcoin use overall is described as limited, though interest may grow along with rising incomes from the oil boom (Sigma).
privacy: Guyana has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Guyana also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.50, ranked 80 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.093, ranked 102 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is spending.

name: Haiti
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are limited and there are no bitcoin on-ramps. Gang violence has closed many bank branches and made cash scarce in Port-au-Prince, and there are no local bitcoin exchanges, so bitcoin users rely on peer-to-peer trades, often paid with the MonCash mobile wallet (Reuters; Le Relief Haiti).
legal: Bitcoin is legal but unregulated. Haiti has passed no bitcoin law and has not banned it; the central bank only talked about a digital currency of its own in 2019. Individuals can hold and use bitcoin, but there is no legal protection and enforcement is weak (Freeman Law).
residency: Moving here is not realistic for most people. Residence permits exist on paper, but armed gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the main airport has faced repeated closures and many governments advise against all travel (US State Department; Reuters).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. We found no regular network of shops taking it; the main grassroots project, Yes Bitcoin Haiti, is still focused on education rather than merchant payments (Blink 2024).
community: There is a small bitcoin community. Yes Bitcoin Haiti, based in Saint Michel de l'Attalaye, runs bitcoin education with the open-source Bitcoin Diploma and appeared at Adopting Bitcoin 2025, but there are no regular public meetups listed (Blink; Adopting Bitcoin 2025; Trezor Academy).
privacy: Haiti has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Haiti also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.

Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.755, ranked 142 of 163 countries.

name: Holy See (Vatican City State)
tax: Vatican City has no specific tax on bitcoin, and we found no tax on bitcoin gains for its few residents. Note that anyone who is tax resident in Italy (most people who work there) falls under Italian tax rules instead. (MEXC 2025)
banking: The only local bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion, serves clergy, Holy See staff and Church bodies and does not deal in bitcoin. In practice, residents use Italian banks just outside the walls. (Holy See; TaxRavens 2026)
legal: Holding bitcoin is not banned, but Vatican law (Law No. XVIII) prohibits providing bitcoin services inside the state, including issuing, exchanging, storing or brokering virtual currencies. The financial watchdog has set up working groups to assess the risks from unlawful bitcoin service providers. (Vatican Supervisory and Financial Information Authority, Annual Report 2025)
residency: Residence is only granted to people who hold roles with the Holy See, such as clergy, Swiss Guards and some staff, plus their families. There is no route for anyone else. (Holy See; TaxRavens 2026)
spending: We found no places inside Vatican City that accept bitcoin. Nearby Rome has a few merchants.
community: There is no bitcoin community inside Vatican City. The nearest meetups are in Rome. (Meetup listings 2026)
privacy: Vatican City has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: the coming EU-aligned rules are scheduled, but decisions rest with a small central authority. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.

name: Honduras
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are effectively off-limits for bitcoin. In February 2024 the banking regulator (CNBS) barred all the banks and financial firms it supervises from holding, investing in, intermediating or operating with bitcoin, so people buy and sell bitcoin through exchanges and person-to-person deals rather than through their bank (CNBS resolution via Cointelegraph).
legal: Owning and using bitcoin is not illegal, but there is no bitcoin law. The Central Bank of Honduras warns that bitcoin is not backed or regulated and that anyone using it does so at their own risk, and banks are banned from bitcoin activity. The Próspera special zone on Roatán treats bitcoin as legal tender and says the bank ban does not apply there, but the government wants to abolish these zones (Central Bank of Honduras and CNBS via CriptoNoticias and Cointelegraph).
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. The pensionado route needs a foreign pension of US$1,500 a month, and the rentista route needs US$2,500 a month (Migration Law 2003; Rio Times Sep 2026).
spending: There are a couple of known spots rather than everyday acceptance. Santa Lucía, a mountain town near Tegucigalpa, launched as 'Bitcoin Valley' in 2022 with about 60 businesses set to take bitcoin, and Próspera on Roatán uses bitcoin as legal tender. We found no recent figures showing how many of these merchants still accept it (CriptoNoticias).
community: The community is small. Groups such as Blockchain Honduras and the exchange Coincaex helped launch Bitcoin Valley, and there are bitcoin-minded residents in Próspera, but we found no regular public bitcoin meetups in the main cities (CriptoNoticias).
privacy: Honduras has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Honduras also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.41, ranked 116 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.075, ranked 96 of 163 countries.

name: Hong Kong
tax: Hong Kong has no capital gains tax, so gains on bitcoin held as a long-term investment are not taxed. Very frequent or business-like trading can be taxed as business profit.
banking: Everyday bitcoin access runs through licensed trading platforms, which have proper banking relationships, and several digital banks support transfers to them. Many traditional banks remain cautious about sending money to unlicensed or overseas exchanges.
legal: Holding and storing bitcoin is legal. Since 2023, retail trading has had to go through licensed platforms, and there is a separate licence for stablecoin issuers.
residency: Residency usually requires a job offer, a recognised talent profile or a large investment, and housing costs are among the highest in the world.
spending: There are some shops, bitcoin ATMs and over-the-counter shops, but most bitcoin activity in Hong Kong is investment rather than everyday payments.
community: Hong Kong is one of Asia's biggest bitcoin centres, with major conferences, exchanges and investment funds.
privacy: Hong Kong has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Hong Kong, that is Hong Kong's own tax office. Because Hong Kong taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Hong Kong's rule of law 24th out of 143 countries, and its dollar has been tied to the US dollar since 1983. Political freedoms have narrowed since 2020. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Hong Kong offers no tax on long-term gains, a well-regulated market and one of Asia's biggest bitcoin scenes. Residency and living costs are the main barriers.

name: Hungary
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate. Since the 2022 reform, annual net bitcoin income is taxed at 15%, and in most cases no social tax is due (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025; CMS).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. The White Card for digital nomads requires about €2,000–3,000 a month, and a Guest Investor golden visa is also available (wheretonomad; immigrantinvest).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in Budapest, but it is not mainstream. The number of businesses accepting bitcoin here is modest compared with the leading countries (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, with meetups and startups. No major bitcoin conference takes place here, and Hungary is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Hungary, that is Hungary's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.50, ranked 79 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.538, ranked 15 of 163 countries.

community: Iceland is known for bitcoin mining thanks to cheap geothermal and hydro power, but the community of everyday bitcoin users is small, with only occasional informal meetups in Reykjavík.

Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

name: India
