banking: Banks are wary of bitcoin, so moving money to and from exchanges is difficult and unreliable. UPI, the national instant payment system run by NPCI, has been withdrawn from bitcoin exchanges since 2022, and SBI has blocked payments to exchanges. Deposits go through a few net-banking partners and person-to-person trades, and we found no sign of this changing in 2026 (Business Standard; Inc42; Forkast).
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. You can legally hold and trade it, but there is no specific bitcoin law. Companies offering bitcoin assets must register under the anti-money-laundering law (PMLA), and new bitcoin reporting under Section 285BAA applies from the 2026-27 financial year (Crypto Times Sep 2026).
residency: Moving here is hard unless you have Indian roots. An employment visa generally needs a salary above US$25,000 a year from an Indian employer, tourist e-visas are capped at 90 or 180 days per visit, and there is no general investor or retirement route. People of Indian origin can get an Overseas Citizen of India card, a lifelong visa. (IndiaLaw 2025; Aniday 2026)
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin: about 166 listed businesses for a population of 1.4 billion (Coinpedia).
community: There is a large, lively bitcoin community with regular events, and the country ranked 6th of 117 for everyday bitcoin use in Chainalysis's 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index. It has a huge community of everyday traders and a strong developer presence despite tax pressure. Opinion is divided because of friction over regulation and tax.

name: Iran, Islamic Republic of

banking: Banks only connect to local exchanges that plug into a central bank system giving the government full access to user data, and the central bank has repeatedly cut off bitcoin payment gateways. Since June 2026 the main exchanges, including Nobitex, are under US sanctions, and international banking is largely closed off. (Central Bank of Iran; US Treasury 2026)
legal: Holding and trading bitcoin on approved local exchanges is tolerated, but paying for goods in bitcoin is banned, bitcoin advertising has been banned since February 2025, and licensed miners must sell their coins to the central bank. name: Liechtenstein
tax: Liechtenstein does not tax private gains from bitcoin, although your holdings count towards wealth tax.
banking: Bank Frick offers regulated bitcoin trading and storage under Liechtenstein's blockchain law.
legal: Liechtenstein has its own blockchain law and has applied the EU's bitcoin rules since February 2025. Individuals are completely free to use bitcoin.
residency: Living here is very hard to arrange: only around 100 independent-means permits are issued a year, and citizenship normally takes 30 years.
spending: Few shops accept bitcoin, and the bitcoin sector is mostly institutional.
community: Liechtenstein has a strong blockchain industry for its size.
privacy: Liechtenstein has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2027 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Liechtenstein, that is Liechtenstein's own tax office. Because Liechtenstein taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks. Residents must also declare the value of their bitcoin every year for wealth tax.
stability: Liechtenstein is extremely stable, uses the Swiss franc and has very consistent bitcoin rules. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Liechtenstein offers excellent bitcoin banking, clear laws and top-class stability, but residency is almost impossible to obtain.

These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Lithuania, that is Lithuania's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

name: Luxembourg

These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Luxembourg, that is Luxembourg's own tax office. name: Macao

banking: Banks in Macao are told to stay away from bitcoin. The Monetary Authority of Macao has reminded all banks and payment institutions not to provide financial services for virtual currency trading, directly or indirectly, citing money laundering risks. In practice this means you should not expect a local bank to handle exchange transfers (Monetary Authority of Macao via Macau Business).
legal: Owning bitcoin is not banned, but it has no legal standing. The Monetary Authority of Macao says bitcoin is neither legal tender nor a financial instrument it supervises, warns about money laundering risks, and has told banks not to offer bitcoin trading services (Monetary Authority of Macao via Macau Business).
residency: Moving to Macao is hard for most foreigners. The main routes are a job with a local employer or a talent scheme with a three-year renewable permit for highly qualified professionals in sectors such as finance, health and technology, capped at around 1,000 places a year in the quota-based tiers, which replaced the older investor and skilled-staff regime (Macau Business).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere to spend bitcoin. We found no reports of shops or restaurants in Macao accepting it, and banks are told not to serve bitcoin trading (Macau Business).
community: The bitcoin community is small and low-profile. We found no regular bitcoin meetups or events in Macao.
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Macau, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.

name: Madagascar

name: Malawi
tax: Malawi has no specific bitcoin tax rules. Its income tax law does tax capital gains for individuals (the gain is worked out after adjusting the purchase cost for inflation), and residents pay income tax at rates from 0% to 35%. The only exemption we found is for shares on the Malawi Stock Exchange held over a year, so bitcoin gains could be taxable, but how this is applied to bitcoin in practice is unclear. (PwC tax summaries 2026)
banking: Banks are effectively closed to bitcoin. The Reserve Bank of Malawi has said since 2018 that it will not approve bitcoin-related foreign-exchange flows, and no bank works with a bitcoin exchange. People rely on mobile money, person-to-person trades or offshore accounts (Blockspot 2026; ITWeb).
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but unregulated. There is no bitcoin law or licensing system, and the Reserve Bank of Malawi has repeatedly warned (2018 to 2024) that bitcoin is not legal tender and that users have no protection, while saying a ban would only push activity underground (Blockspot 2026; ITWeb).
residency: Moving here needs a job, family tie or real investment. The Business Residence Permit asks for at least 50,000 US dollars invested in a productive business and lasts five years, renewable; permanent residence is also open to retirees with an assured income (Visa Atlas).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. We found no shops or businesses taking bitcoin; bitcoin use so far is mostly in education workshops (Blockspot 2026; Blink 2026).
community: There is a small but growing bitcoin community. The group Bitcoin Boma ran a free three-session bitcoin course at a Blantyre university in 2025 with over 130 attendees and held Africa Bitcoin Day in Lilongwe in May 2026, and the Africa Bitcoin Conference is scheduled for Blantyre on 2 to 5 December 2026 (Luma; Africa Bitcoin Conference).
privacy: Malawi has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Bitcoin gains are still taxed, so you need to declare them yourself.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.52, ranked 71 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.994, ranked 82 of 163 countries.

name: Malaysia

name: Marshall Islands

name: Martinique
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Martinique is a French overseas department, so French tax law applies: gains are taxed only once your yearly bitcoin sales exceed €305, and then at the flat tax, which rose from 30% to 31.4% after the 2026 social security budget raised the CSG levy from 9.2% to 10.6% (MoneyVox 2026).
banking: Banking works, but some banks are cautious and transfers may be checked. Martinique uses the euro and the French banking system, and since 1 July 2026 only providers authorised by France's financial markets authority (AMF) under the EU's MiCA rules may serve French clients (83 of 117 French providers were authorised by mid-May 2026). French banks still sometimes question or block transfers to bitcoin platforms, or close accounts as an anti-money-laundering precaution, so using an authorised platform and keeping records helps. (Actu-Juridique Sep 2026; Cryptoactu Jun 2026)
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. Everyone else needs a French long-stay visa or residence permit through the usual French routes such as work, family or study. Note that Martinique is outside the Schengen area: a Schengen visa does not cover it, and short visits need a separate overseas visa unless you are exempt (French Ministry of the Interior).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, if any. We found no news reports of local shops in Martinique taking bitcoin, so day-to-day life runs on euros by card and cash, and bitcoin spending is mostly limited to online services (our search of local and French news, October 2026).
community: There is very little visible bitcoin community. We found no regular bitcoin meetups or events in Fort-de-France; local bitcoiners mostly connect through the wider French community online (our search of local and French news, October 2026).
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Martinique, that is Martinique's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

We found no investor, retirement or digital-nomad visa, so living here usually depends on a job or business link (WhereToEmigrate; CCME).

name: Mauritius
tax: Mauritius has no capital gains tax, so personal bitcoin gains are not taxed unless they amount to business income.
banking: Mauritius licenses bitcoin firms under its 2021 virtual asset law, and the Bank of Mauritius issued guidelines in 2024 for banks dealing with bitcoin businesses. Even so, most banks are still reluctant to work with bitcoin businesses, and licensed exchanges cannot yet use a local bank account to take customer deposits for trading. Individuals mostly buy through international exchanges by card or bank transfer, or person-to-person, and local guides warn that P2P trades can lead to account freezes. (Intercontinental Trust 2025; CMS Expert Guide 2025; Newhedge)
legal: Mauritius was one of Africa's first countries to pass a dedicated bitcoin law, in force since 2022. Its financial regulator licenses bitcoin businesses and issued rules for stablecoins in August 2026.
residency: Mauritius has some of Africa's most accessible residence routes. A self-employed occupation permit needs a USD 35,000 transfer, an investor permit USD 100,000 into your company, and a professional permit a monthly salary of at least MUR 60,000 (MUR 30,000 in IT/outsourcing); complete applications are processed in about five working days. People aged 50 or over can also get a residence permit by bringing in at least USD 1,500 a month. (Economic Development Board Mauritius)
spending: Paying with bitcoin in everyday shops is rare in Mauritius. The few examples we found are online, such as a hotel booking site that started taking bitcoin in 2019, and the bitcoin sector here is focused on licensed financial services rather than shop payments. (Unlock Blockchain 2019; Newhedge)
community: Port Louis hosted the Africa Bitcoin Circular Economies Summit in December 2025, organised with El Salvador's Bitcoin Beach. Grassroots bitcoin culture is growing alongside a strong financial-services sector.
privacy: Mauritius has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Mauritius, that is Mauritius's own tax office. Because Mauritius does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, the reports have little practical effect for residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 47th out of 143 countries. The rupee is a moderately stable floating currency, and the bitcoin rules are well established. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 18th of 163 countries.
summary: Mauritius combines no tax on personal bitcoin gains, one of Africa's clearest bitcoin laws and some of the easiest residence permits around. Local banks are still cautious with bitcoin, and everyday bitcoin spending is rare.

(Voyageurs du Monde travel guide; Transak)

tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Bitcoin gains are taxed as income at your marginal rate, up to 39% (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025; Inland Revenue).
banking: Buying and selling bitcoin through local exchanges such as Easy Bitcoin, Swyftx and Kraken works with the main banks for verified customers, though banks run strict anti-money-laundering checks and may ask where large sums came from. The government planned to ban bitcoin ATMs in 2025 but later chose targeted controls instead (New Zealand Ministry of Justice announcements; 1News Jul 2025).
legal: Owning, holding in your own wallet, spending and trading bitcoin is all legal. Bitcoin businesses must register as financial service providers and follow anti-money-laundering rules, and Inland Revenue treats bitcoin as property for tax (IRD; Financial Markets Authority).
residency: Most people move through skilled work, family or investor routes. Since April 2025 the Active Investor Plus visa needs NZ$5 million over three years (Growth category) or NZ$10 million (Balanced), with no English test, and a cheaper business investor route was added later in 2025 (Immigration New Zealand; KPMG Nov 2025).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. The local BTC Map community, NZBitcoiners, is active in 2026 (BTC Map blog).
community: There is an active bitcoin scene, with regular meetups in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, bitcoin-only businesses such as Stacked Bitcoin, and a national bitcoin conference held in Queenstown (Stacked Bitcoin; NZ bitcoin conference listings 2026).
privacy: New Zealand has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2027 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in New Zealand, that is New Zealand's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.83, ranked 5 of 143 countries. Currency: stable, freely floating New Zealand dollar. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.343, ranked 2 of 163 countries.

name: Nicaragua
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are cautious and bitcoin on-ramps are thin, so most people use peer-to-peer trading or foreign exchanges. Since January 2025 the Financial Analysis Unit (UAF) requires bitcoin providers to log and identify the people and IP addresses behind transfers over US$1,000 (CriptoNoticias Jan 2025).
legal: Holding and using bitcoin is legal, but under close state watch. Bitcoin providers now need a Central Bank of Nicaragua licence (May 2025 regulation), and transfers above US$1,000 are monitored, which critics fear could be used against government opponents (García & Bodán Jul 2025; CriptoNoticias Jan 2025).
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. Pensioner residence has a guideline minimum of about US$1,200 a month. The old Law 694 incentives were repealed in 2024, and the rules are now stricter (Rio Times Sep 2026).
spending: Only a handful of businesses, mostly in tourist areas, are known to accept bitcoin, and there is no wider merchant network to rely on (CriptoNoticias).
community: The bitcoin community is small and informal, with no regular public meetups we could find; the political climate discourages visible organising (CriptoNoticias).
privacy: Nicaragua has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Nicaragua also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Less stable: weak rule of law and a real risk of sudden, politically driven changes, despite a steady currency. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.33, ranked 139 of 143 countries. Currency: the córdoba has been held at a fixed rate against the US dollar since 2024. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: new monitoring rules and a US warning in October 2026 about asset confiscations. name: Niger

name: Niue

name: Norfolk Island
tax: Norfolk Island is part of Australia's tax system, so residents pay Australian capital gains tax on bitcoin. Gains are added to your income and taxed at marginal rates of up to 45% (plus the 2% Medicare levy), halved if you held the coins for more than 12 months. (Australian Taxation Office; KPMG 2026)
banking: Banking runs through Australian banks. Local Australian exchanges accept PayID and bank transfers, but some big banks cap or block payments to certain bitcoin exchanges as a scam-prevention measure, so occasional friction is normal. Local branch services on the island are very limited. (Australian bank policies; ASIC)
legal: Australian law applies: individuals can freely buy, hold, self-custody and spend bitcoin. Exchanges must register with AUSTRAC, and the Digital Assets Framework Act passed in April 2026 will require bitcoin platforms to hold a financial services licence. (AUSTRAC; Australian Parliament 2026)
residency: Australian immigration law applies (since the 2016 reforms the island has been fully part of the Australian migration zone), so foreigners need an Australian visa to live here. There is no special or cheaper route; most people qualify only through skilled work, family ties or a large investment. (Australian Department of Home Affairs)
spending: We found no shops and no businesses on the island that advertise bitcoin payments.
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or local groups; the nearest active communities are on the Australian mainland. (Meetup listings 2026)

name: North Macedonia

name: Northern Mariana Islands
tax: The islands use a 'mirror' of the US tax code, and residents file with the local government instead of the IRS. That means US-style tax on bitcoin gains: 0%, 15% or 20% on long-term gains and ordinary income rates on short-term gains, with full reporting. The local government gives substantial rebates on tax from island-sourced income, which can reduce the bill (Congressional Research Service; Global Property Guide).
banking: Local banking is part of the US dollar system, so US-regulated exchanges and bank transfers can generally be used, with standard US compliance checks. We found little specific information on local banks' attitude to bitcoin.
legal: As a US territory, federal rules apply: individuals can hold, self-custody and trade bitcoin, while bitcoin businesses must follow US licensing and anti-money-laundering rules. A local advocacy group, Crypto Frontier, has pushed for the islands to become a bitcoin business hub (Marianas Variety).
residency: US citizens can move here freely, but others need US immigration status. The main local route for foreign workers, the CW-1 permit, is employer-sponsored, capped, valid for a year at a time and runs only until the end of 2029, so it is hard for most foreigners (US Citizenship and Immigration Services).
spending: Almost nowhere accepts bitcoin. With a small, tourism-based economy, we found no evidence of shops accepting it.
community: Interest is small: a Saipan-based group, Crypto Frontier, has given public talks (for example to the Rotary Club of Saipan) to promote bitcoin, but we found no regular bitcoin meetups (Marianas Variety).
privacy: US federal rules apply here, so bitcoin brokers report trades to the US tax office (IRS). These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the Northern Mariana Islands, that is the Northern Mariana Islands's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: US dollar or Swiss franc or fully dollarised – no local-currency risk. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.

name: Norway

DNB says it will question deposits from bitcoin and may ask for proof of origin, and some users report delays or refused transfers (DNB Mar 2026; Finanstilsynet).
legal: Owning, self-custody and using bitcoin is fully legal. The EU's MiCA bitcoin rules apply in Norway from 1 July 2025, so exchanges and other providers need a licence from Finanstilsynet, but individuals face no special limits (Schjødt 2025; Finanstilsynet 2026).
residency: Moving here is hard unless you are an EU or EEA citizen, who can register to live and work freely. Others usually need a skilled job, family ties or study; there is no investor or digital nomad visa (Norwegian Directorate of Immigration UDI).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, mostly in Oslo, and card payments dominate daily life.
community: There is an active bitcoin community with regular meetups such as OsloPlebs and BitDevs Oslo, bitcoin-only companies like Bare Bitcoin, a large bitcoin mining industry, and the bitcoin-friendly Oslo Freedom Forum every year (Meetup; Oslo Freedom Forum).

These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Norway, that is Norway's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks. Residents must also declare the value of their bitcoin every year for wealth tax.

name: Palestine, State of
tax: There are no bitcoin tax rules. Palestinian income tax law (Law No. 8 of 2011) taxes income from any source, at rates of 5%, 10% and a top rate of 15%, but how it applies to bitcoin gains has not been spelled out, so the position is unclear. (PwC tax summaries 2026)

A 2023 Palestine Monetary Authority circular on virtual assets restates the ban on banks and other financial institutions handling bitcoin transactions, and Gaza's banking system has largely collapsed, with cash exchange offices charging 15–22% to turn bitcoin into cash. name: Panama
tax: Panama has no capital gains tax on bitcoin. It only taxes income earned inside Panama, and gains from bitcoin is treated as foreign income, so residents pay nothing on them. Capital gains tax applies only to a few local assets, such as Panamanian property and shares in Panamanian companies. There is no minimum holding period, no wealth tax on your bitcoin, and no need to report foreign income to the tax office.
banking: Banking is one of Panama's biggest strengths. Towerbank has openly welcomed bitcoin users since 2022: it accepts money coming from exchanges, issues a debit card, runs a platform that holds bitcoin and dollars side by side, and has made more than $10 million of bitcoin-backed loans. The state-owned Caja de Ahorros is designing bitcoin accounts of its own.
legal: Nothing in Panamanian law stops you from buying, holding, storing, sending or paying with bitcoin, and you need no licence to do any of it. A 2022 bitcoin law was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2023. The new bills now being discussed are aimed at bitcoin businesses, not at individuals.
residency: Panama has some of the easiest residency routes in the world. Retirees can qualify with a pension of about $1,000 a month. Citizens of around 50 'friendly nations' can qualify with a local job or about $200,000 in property or savings. Investors can get permanent residency in roughly 30 to 45 business days by buying $300,000 of property, a figure expected to rise after 15 October 2026.
spending: Panama City lets people pay taxes, fees, fines, permits and even bus tickets in bitcoin, with a partner bank converting the payment into dollars straight away. Some property developers and agencies also accept bitcoin, although many prefer dollar-backed stablecoins. Shops that take bitcoin exist, but they are not yet found everywhere.
community: Panama City's mayor, Mayer Mizrachi, is one of the most outspoken supporters of bitcoin in the region. He introduced the city's bitcoin payments and has even suggested priority Canal passage for ships that pay in bitcoin. Bitcoin Day Panama brings banks, regulators and enthusiasts together each year, and local groups run regular meetups.
privacy: Panama has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Panama, that is Panama's own tax office. Because Panama does not tax foreign-source income, including gains on bitcoin, the reports have little practical effect for residents. There is no wealth tax and no requirement to declare income earned abroad. Banks do carry out thorough identity checks when you open an account.
stability: Panama has used the US dollar since 1904, so there is no risk of the local currency losing value. It has a long record of peaceful elections, and S&P confirmed its investment-grade rating in September 2026. The weak spot is the court system, which the World Justice Project ranks 73rd out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 80th of 163 countries.
summary: Panama comes top because it scores highly almost everywhere: no capital gains tax on bitcoin, banks that openly serve bitcoin users, complete legal freedom and some of the easiest residency rules in the world. Its weaker spots are court quality and a bitcoin spending scene that is still growing.

name: Paraguay
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. Paraguay taxes personal income mostly on a territorial basis, so gains from bitcoin held and sold through foreign platforms are generally treated as foreign income and not taxed. Unlike Georgia or El Salvador, there is no law or tax-authority ruling that deals with bitcoin specifically, and local personal income tax rates of 8–10% could apply to activity based in Paraguay.
banking: Banks are wary of bitcoin, so moving money in and out can be difficult. Paraguayan banks are conservative with bitcoin-linked transfers, and many residents rely on over-the-counter desks and person-to-person markets to move between bitcoin and guaraníes or dollars.
legal: Bitcoin is legal, and individuals face no restrictions on using it. Paraguay's main bitcoin law covers mining, which is regulated and taxed because it uses hydroelectric power. A broader bitcoin law was attempted in 2022 but vetoed.
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. Temporary and then permanent residency is relatively quick and cheap, and it remains one of the most accessible routes in South America.
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. A small number of businesses in Asunción accept it, but there is no widespread local network of people and shops using bitcoin.
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, shaped by the mining industry, with meetups in Asunción.
privacy: Paraguay has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Paraguay also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Stability here comes down to rule of law (World Justice Project 2025: 0.45, rank 100), currency (the guaraní is relatively stable but not dollarised) and the risk of a sudden policy change (no restrictions on individuals; mining rules target electricity use). Peace and security: the Global Peace Index 2026 scores Paraguay 1.882 (rank 63 of 163).
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is banking.

name: Peru
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, and in most everyday cases zero. Individuals' gains are treated as second-category capital income, with an effective rate of about 6.25% (TaxAtlas Peru page 2026). Cointelegraph reports rates of 8–30% depending on income, so the rules are not fully settled.
banking: Peru has no specific bitcoin law, but bitcoin service providers must register with the financial intelligence unit for anti-money-laundering checks, and banks increasingly work with exchanges. Banco de Credito del Peru, the largest bank, runs a pilot approved by the banking regulator that lets clients buy bitcoin and stablecoins inside the bank. Peru has more than 1.2 million bitcoin users. (Forbes Peru, January 2026)
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. Bitcoin providers are regulated only for anti-money-laundering purposes: under SBS Resolution 02648-2024 they must report to the authorities, but they do not need a licence (soulbit.io).
residency: Moving here is easy and affordable for most people. The Rentista residence permit needs at least US$1,000 a month in passive income (Superintendencia Nacional de Migraciones; WhereNext).
spending: You can spend bitcoin at some places, mainly in grassroots 'circular economy' projects. The non-profit Motiv runs hubs in Lima, Cusco and Huanchaco plus programmes in Tarapoto and Iquitos, and says 25,000 to 30,000 bitcoin payments have come through its work. Outside these pockets, few ordinary shops accept it. (Bitcoin Magazine, February 2026; CriptoNoticias)
community: Peru has an active bitcoin scene. Motiv teaches bitcoin six days a week at about 15 locations and says its events reached more than 6,000 people in 2025. Lima also hosts regular bitcoin conferences, such as the Peru Blockchain Conference in 2026. (Bitcoin Magazine, February 2026; CriptoNoticias)
privacy: Peru has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Peru also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.48, ranked 93 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.120, ranked 106 of 163 countries.
summary: Peru is one of Latin America's rising bitcoin options: a low tax rate on gains, an easy retiree and passive-income visa, and a fast-growing grassroots scene led by the Motiv project in Lima and Cusco. The largest bank is even piloting bitcoin. Bitcoin rules are still light-touch and stability is middling.

name: Philippines
tax: The Philippines charges a 15% tax on gains from selling bitcoin. Mining and staking are taxed as income, and VAT can apply to bitcoin payments.
banking: Buying bitcoin is easy. UnionBank, one of the country's biggest banks, lets customers buy and sell bitcoin in its app. GCash, with about 90 million accounts, and Maya also offer bitcoin inside their apps.
legal: Bitcoin is legal and licensed, but rules tightened in July 2025: platforms serving Filipinos must be local companies. The regulator named ten unregistered overseas exchanges, including OKX, Bybit and Kraken, and they can no longer be funded through GCash.
residency: The Philippines has one of Asia's easiest retirement visas, requiring a pension of about $800 a month plus a $10,000 deposit (from age 40). There is also a digital nomad visa for those earning about $2,000 a month.
spending: Some businesses accept bitcoin, but bitcoin use is mostly about trading rather than shopping.
community: The Philippines ranks 19th in the world for everyday bitcoin use in Chainalysis's 2026 index, with a very strong trading community and positive attitudes to bitcoin.
privacy: The Philippines has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the Philippines, that is the Philippines's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks the country's rule of law 97th out of 143 countries, and the peso is a moderately stable floating currency. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 101st of 163 countries.
summary: The Philippines stands out for very easy bank access to bitcoin and one of Asia's most affordable retirement visas. Tighter platform rules and a 15% tax are the downsides.

name: Pitcairn
tax: Pitcairn has no taxation at all, so there is no tax on bitcoin gains. (Pitcairn Islands Government immigration FAQ)
banking: There is no bank on the island. Residents use banks in New Zealand or elsewhere, so getting money to and from an exchange depends on a foreign bank. (Pitcairn Islands Government)
legal: Bitcoin is not banned, but this British Overseas Territory has no bitcoin rules of its own, so the legal position is simply untested. (Pitcairn Islands Government)
residency: Pitcairn actively invites new settlers. You need savings of at least NZ$30,000, endorsement by the Island Council and an interview with the Deputy Governor, and the fee is NZ$500. Land for a home is granted free on lease. The island is extremely remote, reached only by boat. (Pitcairn Islands Government immigration 2024)
spending: With about 40 residents and a handful of businesses, there is nowhere to spend bitcoin. We found no shops.
community: We found no bitcoin community or meetups on the island. (Meetup listings 2026)
privacy: Pitcairn has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Pitcairn also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the New Zealand dollar. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: no bitcoin rules exist, and any new ones would likely follow UK practice. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for tax and privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Poland
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate. Since 2019, bitcoin gains have been taxed at a flat 19% (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is possible, but you need a job, a business or family ties. EU citizens can move freely. Non-EU citizens usually need a work-based permit or the EU Blue Card (Poland has no separate national permit for highly qualified workers), or a temporary residence permit for running a business, valid up to 3 years, costing PLN 340 plus PLN 100 for the card, with a decision due within 60 days (EU Immigration Portal).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. The number is modest compared with the leading countries: there are visible clusters of accepting businesses in the major cities, but not across the whole country (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: There is an active bitcoin community, with plenty of meetups, events and bitcoin start-ups. Warsaw hosts the Bitcoin FilmFest (bitcoinconferences.info). Poland is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Poland, that is Poland's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.66, ranked 32 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.615, ranked 22 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for banking, legal freedom, community and stability. Weakest areas are tax, residency, spending and privacy.

name: Portugal
tax: Since 2023, gains on bitcoin held for more than a year are tax-free for individuals in Portugal. Gains on bitcoin held for less than a year are taxed at a flat 28%, and staking or professional trading falls under normal income tax.
banking: Portugal uses the EU's standard bank-transfer system. Banks generally accept money coming from regulated exchanges if you can show the paperwork, although some banks are more welcoming than others.
legal: The EU's bitcoin rules apply. Individuals are free to hold and use bitcoin, but platforms must record details of transfers to and from personal wallets.
residency: Portugal's passive-income (D7) visa and digital nomad visa are open to people with a modest monthly income, and a 'golden visa' is still available through investment funds.
spending: Lisbon and Madeira have visible clusters of businesses that accept bitcoin, supported by a large community of people who have moved there.
community: Portugal has one of Europe's largest communities of bitcoiners who have relocated there, with frequent meetups and conferences and a lively digital-nomad scene.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Portugal, that is Portugal's own tax office. Because Portugal taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Portugal uses the euro and the World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 29th out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 7th of 163 countries.
summary: Portugal pairs tax-free long-term bitcoin gains with accessible visas, a large international bitcoin community and EU stability. Gains on bitcoin held for less than a year are taxed at 28%.

name: Puerto Rico
tax: US citizens who genuinely move to Puerto Rico can pay 0% local tax on capital gains made after the move, if they apply for the Act 60 tax decree by 31 December 2026. From 2027, new applicants are set to pay 4%, subject to final approval. Only US citizens benefit, and there are yearly donation and property requirements.
banking: Puerto Rico uses the US banking system, with full access to US exchanges, bitcoin funds and storage providers, under strict US rules.
legal: US federal law applies, and individuals are free to hold and use bitcoin.
residency: Puerto Rico is open to US citizens without any visa. People from other countries need US immigration status, which is hard to get.
spending: San Juan has a cluster of bitcoin-accepting businesses, helped by the many bitcoiners who have moved there.
community: Puerto Rico has a large community of bitcoiners who have relocated there and hosts frequent events.
privacy: US federal rules apply here, so bitcoin brokers report trades to the US tax office (IRS). These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Puerto Rico, that is Puerto Rico's own tax office. Because Puerto Rico taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Puerto Rico operates within the US legal system and uses the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: For US citizens, Puerto Rico is a unique option: 0% local tax on new gains (for decrees applied for in 2026), US banking and a big bitcoin community. For everyone else, residency is difficult.

name: Qatar
tax: You pay no tax on bitcoin gains here as an individual. There is no personal income tax or capital gains tax, so bitcoin gains are not taxed for individuals (TaxAtlas crypto-tax table 2026).
banking: Banks are not allowed, or not willing, to deal with bitcoin. The Qatar Central Bank bars financial institutions from dealing in bitcoin (taxinme.com).
legal: Bitcoin is restricted: you may be able to hold it, but using or trading it is limited. The Qatar Central Bank bans financial institutions from trading bitcoin, and the Qatar Financial Centre's rules cover only investment tokens (taxinme.com 2026).
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. Buying property worth about US$200,000 gets a renewable residence permit, and about US$1 million gets permanent residency (Gulf News; Khaleej Times).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. The central bank has barred banks from bitcoin dealings since 2018, bitcoin services have been banned in the Qatar Financial Centre since 2020, and the 2024 digital assets rules cover only tokenised shares and bonds, not bitcoin. (Lightspark; The Block)
community: The bitcoin community is small and low-key. Bitcoin services are banned locally, and we found no regular bitcoin meetups in Doha, so people in the region tend to go to events in Abu Dhabi or Dubai instead. (Lightspark)
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Qatar, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.62, ranked 41 of 143 countries. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.676, ranked 31 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax. Weakest areas are banking and spending.

name: Romania
tax: Romania taxes bitcoin gains at a flat 10%, one of the lowest rates in the EU, with a small exemption for minor transactions.
banking: Like the rest of the EU, residents can use banks such as Revolut, N26 and bunq that sell bitcoin inside their apps, and send money to licensed exchanges by ordinary bank transfer. Local banks vary in how welcoming they are, and large transfers may be checked.
legal: The EU's bitcoin rules have applied fully since the end of 2024. Individuals are free to hold, store in their own wallets and trade bitcoin, although platforms must record details of transfers to and from personal wallets.
residency: Romania's digital nomad visa needs an income of about €3,300 to €4,000 a month.
spending: Some businesses in the cities accept bitcoin, but the number is modest compared with the leading countries.
community: Romania has an active everyday bitcoin community with exchanges and meetups, although no major bitcoin conference takes place here.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Romania, that is Romania's own tax office. Because Romania taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Romania's rule of law 44th out of 143 countries, and the leu is a moderately stable currency. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks Romania 45th of 163 countries.
summary: Romania offers a low 10% bitcoin tax, EU legal certainty and a reasonably peaceful environment. Residency needs a solid income, and bitcoin spending is still limited.

name: Russian Federation
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a moderate rate of about 15% (TaxAtlas crypto-tax table 2026).
banking: Banks are wary of bitcoin, so moving money in and out can be difficult. A new law routes bitcoin purchases through firms registered with the Bank of Russia, with limits for ordinary buyers. Banks are only starting limited bitcoin services, and businesses that accept bitcoin face fines and frozen accounts (KuCoin Aug 2026; Bitcoin Magazine).
legal: Bitcoin is restricted. Under a law signed on 4 August 2026 (in force from 1 September 2026), bitcoin counts as property, but ordinary investors are capped at about RUB 300,000 a year per provider and paying with bitcoin inside the country is still banned. Transfers above RUB 100,000 to your own wallet face a 48-hour waiting period (KuCoin; CoinMarketCap; Bank of Russia).
residency: Residence is possible but comes with strings. Citizens of 47 mostly Western countries can apply for a 'shared values' visa, followed by a three-year temporary residence permit with no quota and no Russian language test. You must live in your chosen region and spend no more than 180 days a year abroad. Russia issued 1,112 such visas in 2025. Other routes usually need a job, family or a quota. (Russia Beyond, 2025; Meduza, June 2026)
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. Domestic bitcoin payments remain banned under the 2026 law, which also bans advertising bitcoin payments for goods and services (CoinMarketCap; unlock-bc).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events. Russia ranks 16th of 117 countries for everyday bitcoin use in Chainalysis's 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index. It has a large everyday and underground bitcoin community and a mining culture, and attitudes are positive, with bitcoin also used to get around sanctions.
privacy: Russia closely monitors financial activity or limits money leaving the country, and bitcoin use is watched or restricted by the authorities.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.41, ranked 119 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 3.367, ranked 162 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for community. Weakest area is spending.

name: Rwanda
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks have long been cautious after National Bank of Rwanda warnings about bitcoin, and there are no established local exchanges yet, so most people use peer-to-peer trading or foreign platforms. The new 2026 virtual asset law should allow licensed on-ramps over time (National Bank of Rwanda; Capital Market Authority).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. Law No. 023/2026 Regulating Virtual Asset Business was passed in May 2026 (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: Rwanda is open to visitors, with visas on arrival for all nationalities, and residence permits are available for jobs, investors, business owners and retirees through a quick online system, but you still need a job, business or proof of income (Rwanda Directorate General of Immigration and Emigration).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin; we found little or no evidence of shops taking it.
community: The bitcoin community is small but growing, mostly tech and fintech circles in Kigali, with occasional events rather than regular meetups.
privacy: Rwanda has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Rwanda also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.63, ranked 39 of 143 countries. Currency: the Rwandan franc steadily loses value against the dollar. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.200, ranked 113 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is spending.

name: Réunion
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Réunion is a French overseas department, so French tax law applies: gains are taxed only once your yearly bitcoin sales exceed €305, and then at the flat tax, which rose from 30% to 31.4% after the 2026 social security budget raised the CSG levy from 9.2% to 10.6% (MoneyVox 2026).
banking: Banking works, but some banks are cautious and transfers may be checked. Réunion uses the euro and the French banking system, and since 1 July 2026 only providers authorised by France's financial markets authority (AMF) under the EU's MiCA rules may serve French clients (83 of 117 French providers were authorised by mid-May 2026). French banks still sometimes question or block transfers to bitcoin platforms, or close accounts as an anti-money-laundering precaution, so using an authorised platform and keeping records helps. (Actu-Juridique Sep 2026; Cryptoactu Jun 2026)
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Residency follows French law, so EU citizens can move here freely. Everyone else needs a French long-stay visa or residence permit through the usual French routes such as work, family or study. Note that Réunion is outside the Schengen area: a Schengen visa does not cover it, and short visits need a separate overseas visa unless you are exempt (French Ministry of the Interior).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, if any. We found no news reports of local shops in Réunion taking bitcoin, so day-to-day life runs on euros by card and cash, and bitcoin spending is mostly limited to online services. The Banque de France notes that people on Réunion still use cash more than in mainland France, although card use in shops is now very similar (Banque de France 2024).
community: There is very little visible bitcoin community. We found no regular bitcoin meetups or events in Saint-Denis or Saint-Pierre; local bitcoiners mostly connect through the wider French community online (our search of local and French news, October 2026).
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Réunion, that is Réunion's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the euro. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: EU-wide MiCA rules give a stable framework, though French tax on gains has changed, most recently in 2026. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are tax, spending, community and privacy.

name: Saint Barthélemy
tax: Saint Barthélemy has its own tax code and no personal income tax for qualifying residents, so bitcoin gains are generally untaxed. The catch: people moving from mainland France are only treated as local tax residents after five years on the island, and until then French tax (30% on bitcoin gains) can still apply; French social charges may also still apply (Pebbles 2026).
banking: Local banking is small: card payments are common and there are cash machines in Gustavia and St Jean, but we found no evidence of local banks serving bitcoin users, so most people rely on banks and exchanges elsewhere (Gustavia Harbor).
legal: Holding and using bitcoin is legal and we found no restrictions on individuals. Saint Barthélemy runs its own tax system, and it uses the euro (Pebbles 2026; Gustavia Harbor).
residency: Moving here is difficult and very expensive. Foreign nationals may need a residence permit and must register locally, showing housing, means and health insurance, and housing on this luxury island is scarce and costly (Pebbles 2026).
spending: There is almost nowhere to spend bitcoin. Payments on the island are in euros or US dollars by card or cash, and we found no shops reported to accept bitcoin (Gustavia Harbor).
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups, groups or events in Saint Barthélemy.
privacy: Saint Barthélemy has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Saint Barthélemy also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the euro. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
tax: St Helena has its own income tax (26% to 31% for individuals), but its capital gains tax applies only to land, buildings and business stakes with a St Helena link, so gains from simply holding bitcoin generally fall outside it. Frequent trading as a business could be taxed as income, and there is no official bitcoin guidance (St Helena Government; Income Tax Ordinance).
banking: The Bank of St Helena is the only bank on the island and offers no bitcoin services. Moving money to and from exchanges usually means using a UK or other overseas bank account.
legal: Bitcoin is not banned. These UK Overseas Territories have no bitcoin law, so individuals can hold it, but there is no local regulation or guidance.
residency: Non-Saints need an entry permit and then a residence permit, usually tied to a job, a business investment or family. Ascension has no right of abode, and Tristan da Cunha does not allow outsiders to settle (St Helena Government).
spending: We found no shops or businesses on St Helena, Ascension or Tristan da Cunha that accept bitcoin.
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or groups in these territories.
privacy: Saint Helena has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Saint Helena also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
tax: Saint Kitts and Nevis has no personal income tax and no capital gains tax, so individuals pay nothing on bitcoin gains.
banking: Banking is the weak spot. The regional central bank urges people to treat bitcoin as high-risk, we found no local bank openly offering bitcoin services, and Caribbean banks are under pressure from international partner banks to avoid risky clients.
legal: Individuals are free to own and trade bitcoin. Bitcoin businesses are regulated under the Virtual Asset Act of 2020, which was updated in 2021, 2024 and 2026, and new Virtual Asset Business Regulations were issued in 2026; anti-money-laundering rules apply to these businesses. (Financial Services Regulatory Commission St Kitts and Nevis; Library of Congress 2021)
residency: Saint Kitts and Nevis runs one of the oldest citizenship-by-investment programmes, with a minimum of around $200,000.
spending: Around 200 businesses and four ATMs accepted bitcoin in 2022, mostly Bitcoin Cash. BTC Map shows no sign of recent activity, so these figures may be out of date.
community: The islands hosted a bitcoin conference with the Prime Minister in 2022, and there is a small but active bitcoin-aware expat community. We found no bitcoin events planned for 2026.
privacy: Saint Kitts and Nevis has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Saint Kitts and Nevis also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 40th out of 143 countries, and the Eastern Caribbean dollar is firmly tied to the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Saint Kitts and Nevis offers zero tax, fast citizenship and good privacy. Banking for bitcoin users is difficult, and everyday bitcoin use is limited.

name: Saint Lucia
tax: Saint Lucia has no capital gains tax, so personal bitcoin gains are not taxed unless they amount to business income.
banking: Banking is the weak spot. The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank urges people to treat bitcoin as high-risk, we found no local bank openly offering bitcoin services, and Caribbean banks are under pressure from international partner banks to avoid risky clients.
legal: Owning, holding and using bitcoin is legal for individuals. Since the Virtual Asset Business Act was passed in December 2022, anyone running a bitcoin business in or from Saint Lucia must be licensed by the Financial Services Regulatory Authority, mainly as an anti-money-laundering measure, but there are no special restrictions on private holders. (Government of Saint Lucia; Attorney General's Chambers)
residency: Saint Lucia offers citizenship by investment from about $240,000.
spending: We found no recent data on businesses accepting bitcoin, and the regional central bank discourages using bitcoin for payments.
community: There are small bitcoin interest groups, but we found no bitcoin conferences or community projects planned for 2026.
privacy: Saint Lucia has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Saint Lucia also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 43rd out of 143 countries, and the Eastern Caribbean dollar is firmly tied to the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Saint Lucia offers zero tax on personal gains, a straightforward citizenship programme and good privacy. Banking and everyday bitcoin use remain limited.

name: Saint Martin (French part)
tax: Saint Martin has set its own taxes since 2007, with an income tax broadly modelled on France's. But anyone moving from France or a French overseas department stays taxed under French state rules for their first five years, and France taxes bitcoin gains at a flat 31.4% from 2026 (sales under 305 euros a year are exempt). How the island's own code treats bitcoin for long-term residents is not clearly published. (French Senate report; Waltio 2026)
banking: Local banking is limited. Residents can use bitcoin services licensed under EU rules, but we found no evidence of local banks openly serving bitcoin users.
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Saint Martin follows French immigration rules. People from outside the EU usually need a French long-stay visa or residence permit, and we found no special route for this territory.
spending: Prices are in euros and US dollars. Bitcoin is accepted at only a handful of venues on the island, such as one nightclub, and is far less common than cash or cards. (Sotheby's International Realty St Martin)
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or community groups on the French side of the island.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, that is Saint Vincent and the Grenadines's own tax office. Because Saint Vincent and the Grenadines does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, the reports have little practical effect for residents. name: Samoa

banking: Banks are cautious with bitcoin. Bitcoin is among the sectors most likely to face extra checks or account refusals, no local bank is known to serve bitcoin exchanges, and Samoa's past place on the EU tax blacklist (it was removed in February 2026) still makes foreign banks wary, so most people rely on foreign platforms or peer-to-peer trades (Expanship 2026).
legal: Holding bitcoin is not banned, but the rules are strict and still developing. The Central Bank says bitcoin is not legal tender and calls it speculative and high-risk, anyone promoting virtual currency needs Central Bank approval under anti-money-laundering law, and bitcoin businesses need a licence, while simply holding and trading for yourself is not licensed. The Central Bank regularly warns about bitcoin scams, most recently in March 2026 (Samoa News Hub 2026; Expanship 2026).

The usual route is a work permit sponsored by a Samoan employer who must show no local can fill the job; the alternative is the Citizenship by Investment scheme, which needs a SAT$4 million investment and SAT$2.5 million net worth, and ordinary permanent residence usually takes 10 or more years (Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Labour; Rivermate).

community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups, groups or events in Samoa; most bitcoin news there is about scam warnings from the Central Bank (Samoa News Hub 2026).

name: Serbia

tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks offer no bitcoin services. The Central Bank of Somalia said in June 2024 that no financial institution in the country is licensed for bitcoin, so people who use bitcoin rely on peer-to-peer trades, usually settled through mobile money like EVC Plus (Central Bank of Somalia public notice, June 2024).
legal: Bitcoin sits in a grey area. It is not banned, but the Central Bank of Somalia's June 2024 notice says bitcoin is not legal tender, no bitcoin service providers are licensed and the public should avoid investing or trading in it (Central Bank of Somalia, June 2024).
residency: Moving here is very difficult. Work permits exist for people sponsored by employers or aid organisations, but ongoing conflict with al-Shabaab makes Somalia impractical for almost everyone (UK and US travel advice).
spending: You will struggle to find anywhere that accepts bitcoin. We found no shops; everyday payments in Somalia run on dollar-based mobile money instead.
community: There is very little visible bitcoin community. Bitcoin is used informally, and both the Central Bank of Somalia and the Bank of Somaliland have warned about bitcoin scams, but we found no regular bitcoin meetups (Central Bank of Somalia 2024; Somaliland Chronicle 2024).

name: South Africa
tax: South Africa taxes bitcoin gains as capital gains for most investors. The first R40,000 each year is tax-free, rising to R50,000 from the 2027 tax year, and only 40% of the rest is taxed, so the highest effective rate is 18%. Active traders can be taxed as income at up to 45%.
banking: South Africa has a large licensed bitcoin market, with around 300 companies approved by the financial regulator. MoneyBadger lets people pay in bitcoin through the Scan to Pay banking network.
legal: Bitcoin is regulated as a financial product, and bitcoin businesses need a licence from the financial regulator. Individuals are free to use bitcoin.
residency: South Africa's digital nomad visa needs an income of about $2,900 a month and can last up to 36 months.
spending: South Africa is one of the easiest places in the world to spend bitcoin. Through MoneyBadger, about 650,000 shops can accept it, including every Pick n Pay supermarket. BTC Map recorded 918 new locations in 2025, second only to the United States.
community: South Africa ranks ninth in the world for everyday bitcoin use in Chainalysis's 2026 index and has one of Africa's strongest bitcoin communities, with exchanges, payment start-ups and a lively scene.
privacy: South Africa has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2027 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in South Africa, that is South Africa's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are taxed here, the reports are used to check what you declare. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks South Africa's rule of law 60th out of 143 countries, and the rand is a moderately stable floating currency. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 122nd of 163 countries.
summary: South Africa is the best place in the world to actually spend bitcoin, with hundreds of thousands of shops accepting it and a thriving community. Moderate tax and banks that apply extra checks are the trade-offs.

name: South Sudan
tax: South Sudan has no specific tax on bitcoin. But the central bank has told people not to deal in bitcoin at all, so you cannot legally benefit from this (Sudans Post).
banking: Banks will not help you with bitcoin. The Bank of South Sudan has told citizens not to deal in bitcoin, there is no local exchange, and the banking system itself is fragile, with the pound trading at about 4,450 per US dollar officially and 5,500 on the street in early 2025 (Sudans Post; Eye Radio; Blockspot 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is effectively banned. In October 2022 the central bank governor issued a statement prohibiting citizens from dealing in virtual currencies, saying they have no legal status and users have no legal protection (Sudans Post).
residency: There is no realistic route for most foreigners to settle here. The country faces conflict and a deep economic crisis, and we found no residence route aimed at investors, retirees or remote workers.
spending: We found no shops or businesses in South Sudan that accept bitcoin (Blockspot 2026).
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or organised groups in South Sudan; any bitcoin use is small, informal person-to-person trading (Blockspot 2026).

name: Spain
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. They fall under savings-income bands of 19–30%, and from 2025 the top 30% rate applies to gains above EUR 300,000 (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Banks openly work with bitcoin users, so buying and selling through your bank is easy. BBVA opened bitcoin and ether trading to all adult retail customers on 4 July 2025, and Openbank also sells bitcoin (cryptocardtools).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. The digital nomad visa needs an income of €2,849 a month (citizenremote).
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. About 117 businesses are listed as accepting it (Coinpedia).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events, plus a strong bitcoin start-up scene. Madrid hosts the MadBitcoin Summit, which has a 2026 edition (Bitfinity conference guide; Forbes 2026 list).
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Spain, that is Spain's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks. Residents with larger holdings must also declare them for wealth tax, and bitcoin held abroad above EUR 50,000 must be reported.

name: Sri Lanka

banking: Banks are wary of bitcoin. The Central Bank says only the rupee may be used for payments at home and plans to make bitcoin businesses register with its Financial Intelligence Unit over money-laundering concerns, so many people rely on foreign exchanges and peer-to-peer trades. (Ada Derana, September 2025; Daily Mirror, September 2025)
legal: Owning and investing in bitcoin is not illegal, because no law covers it yet, but the Central Bank Governor said in September 2025 that bitcoin cannot be used to pay for things inside the country. New rules requiring bitcoin businesses to register with the Financial Intelligence Unit are being prepared. (Ada Derana, September 2025; Daily Mirror, September 2025)
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. The digital nomad visa requires $2,000–3,250 a month (globalcitizensolutions).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin. In November 2025 Bybit Pay and local firm Ceylon Cash announced a scheme to equip 100 merchants (50 shops and 50 online stores), but the Central Bank says bitcoin should not be used for domestic payments, so everyday spending stays rare. (MEA Tech Watch, November 2025; Ada Derana, September 2025)

privacy: Sri Lanka has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Sri Lanka also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.51, ranked 74 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.910, ranked 66 of 163 countries.

name: Suriname
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are cautious and the central bank says it cannot vouch for bitcoin transactions. There are no licensed local exchanges yet, so people mostly buy and sell through over-the-counter brokers, peer-to-peer trades or a few bitcoin ATMs, and around a quarter of adults are unbanked or underbanked (Central Bank of Suriname via Key News; Bitcoin Sranan report 2025).
legal: Holding and using bitcoin is not banned, but Suriname has no bitcoin law in force. The Central Bank of Suriname has said it is preparing rules for bitcoin service providers in line with international anti-money-laundering standards, and warns the public about volatility and fraud, so there is little consumer protection for now (Key News, December 2023; Bitcoin Sranan report 2025).
residency: There is no digital nomad or easy retirement visa. Long stays need a residence permit based on work, family or business, with permanent residence possible after five years; people of Surinamese origin can get a special status. Expat guides warn the process is paperwork-heavy and not always predictable (Where To Emigrate Suriname guide; Rio Times 2026).
spending: The grassroots group Bitcoin Sranan reports around 125 to 150 merchants taking Lightning payments by late 2025, mainly in Paramaribo, including stalls at the central market and in shopping malls, plus four bitcoin ATMs. Outside the capital acceptance is rare, so you can spend bitcoin some of the time but not rely on it (Bitcoin Sranan report 2025).
community: Suriname has an active grassroots scene led by Bitcoin Sranan, founded in 2022, with monthly meetups on the 21st, education workshops and a bitcoin conference in Paramaribo in March 2026. Wallet sign-ups have grown fast, though the community is still young and small in absolute numbers (Bitcoin Sranan report 2025).

Suriname also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.

Currency: the Surinamese dollar lost most of its value in 2020–2023 when inflation topped 50%; inflation has since eased and the rate is around 37–38 per US dollar in 2026, but it remains a soft currency. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: bitcoin rules are still being prepared. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.

name: Svalbard and Jan Mayen
tax: Svalbard has its own lower tax system: people taxed as Svalbard residents pay 16% on non-salary income such as investment gains, plus wealth tax at mainland Norwegian rates. People who move up from mainland Norway usually stay taxable there too, where gains are taxed at 22%. Jan Mayen has no permanent residents (Norwegian Tax Administration; Storting 2026 tax decision).
banking: Banking runs through the Norwegian system. Norwegian banks generally let documented customers move money to and from registered exchanges such as Firi, but some banks ask detailed source-of-funds questions or block transfers to foreign platforms (Norwegian Tax Administration; Finanstilsynet).
legal: Norwegian rules apply in practice: individuals can freely buy, hold and self-custody bitcoin, while bitcoin businesses must be registered with Norway's financial regulator, Finanstilsynet. You must report your bitcoin holdings and gains in your tax return (Finanstilsynet; Norwegian Tax Administration).
residency: Under the Svalbard Treaty, citizens of any treaty country can live and work in Svalbard without a visa or residence permit. In practice you must support yourself, and housing is scarce and usually tied to a job, so most people need an employer first; the Governor can turn away people without means (Governor of Svalbard; VisaAtlas 2026).
spending: We found no shops in Longyearbyen or elsewhere in Svalbard that accept bitcoin.
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or groups in Svalbard.
privacy: Svalbard has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2027 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Svalbard, that is Svalbard's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
