name: Sweden
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Capital gains, including on bitcoin, are taxed at a flat 30%, and only 70% of losses can be deducted (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Most banks let you move money to and from bitcoin platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell bitcoin in their apps across the EU, such as Revolut (licensed under the EU's bitcoin rules, MiCA, via Cyprus, with a Lithuanian bank licence), N26 and bunq, and can send money to EU-licensed exchanges by SEPA bank transfer. How willing local banks are varies, and large transfers can trigger anti-money-laundering checks (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is easy for EU and EEA citizens, but hard for everyone else. Since 1 June 2026 a new work permit needs a salary of at least 90% of the Swedish median, currently SEK 34,470 a month, and there is no investor or digital nomad visa. (Swedish Migration Agency 2026)
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin, and the number is modest compared with the leading countries. Few businesses take it, and people mostly treat bitcoin as an investment (Coinpedia 2026; BTC Map).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events, and a strong community of developers and bitcoin investors. No major bitcoin conference takes place here, and it is not among the 20 most active bitcoin countries in the Chainalysis 2026 index.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Sweden, that is Sweden's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.

Currency: hard peg, euro or a stable major currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.732, ranked 40 of 163 countries.

name: Switzerland
tax: Private investors living in Switzerland pay no tax on bitcoin gains. You must declare your bitcoin each year, and it counts towards a small cantonal wealth tax. Very frequent or large-scale trading can be treated as a business and taxed as income.
banking: Switzerland has the most mature bitcoin banking in the world. Licensed bitcoin banks such as Sygnum and AMINA, cantonal banks and PostFinance all offer bitcoin trading and storage to everyday customers.
legal: Switzerland's 2021 blockchain law created a clear, liberal framework, and individuals face no restrictions on holding, storing, spending or trading bitcoin.
residency: Moving to Switzerland is hard for people from outside the EU. The main routes are employer sponsorship, special lump-sum tax deals or large investments, all subject to local quotas.
spending: Lugano's Plan B programme has nearly 400 businesses accepting bitcoin and lets residents pay city fees in it, while the canton of Zug accepts bitcoin for tax payments. Switzerland has one of the highest densities of bitcoin-accepting places in Europe.
community: Switzerland is home to 'Crypto Valley' in Zug, the Plan B Forum in Lugano, a deep pool of developers and researchers, and many major bitcoin businesses.
privacy: Switzerland has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in Switzerland, that is Switzerland's own tax office. Because Switzerland taxes bitcoin lightly, or not at all in most cases, the reports have little practical effect for most residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks. Residents must also list the value of their bitcoin every year in their wealth-tax return.
stability: Switzerland has excellent rule of law, direct democracy and one of the most stable currencies in the world. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 3rd of 163 countries.
summary: Switzerland is the world's most established home for bitcoin banking and business, with tax-free gains for private investors and outstanding stability. Getting residency is the main hurdle.

name: Syrian Arab Republic

banking: Banking is slowly reconnecting after most US, EU and UK sanctions were lifted in 2025: parts of the system are back on SWIFT, Visa and Mastercard, but withdrawals are still restricted and the central bank says bitcoin trading is illegal. People use Binance (which opened to Syrian residents in June 2025), person-to-person trades and fintech apps instead of banks (EnterpriseAM 2026; Enab Baladi 2025).
legal: Syria has no law that authorises or bans bitcoin, but in August 2025 the Central Bank of Syria said buying and selling bitcoin is illegal and warned users could face prosecution. In practice trading continues openly, so it is a grey area with real enforcement risk (Enab Baladi 2025; EnterpriseAM 2026).
residency: Moving to Syria is very difficult for most foreigners. The country is rebuilding after war, security remains fragile in places, and there is no investor, retirement or remote-work residence route.
spending: We found no shops that accept bitcoin directly. Digital payments are growing through local wallets, but cash remains the norm (EnterpriseAM 2026).
community: A small but growing bitcoin scene exists, mainly around remittances: the local bitcoin and stablecoin payments app Bitknz reports over 18,000 active users. We found no regular public bitcoin meetups (EnterpriseAM 2026).

name: Taiwan, Province of China

banking: Moving money to and from registered local exchanges works well. Bitcoin exchanges must register with the Financial Supervisory Commission under anti-money-laundering rules, and in 2024 the exchange BitoPro teamed up with Far Eastern bank's digital bank Bankee to offer bitcoin-friendly accounts. Expect identity checks, and banks may call to confirm the purpose of incoming foreign transfers (bitcoin.news; law.asia; Taiwan Gold Card community guide).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The Virtual Asset Service Act passed its third reading on 30 June 2026, moving bitcoin businesses from anti-money-laundering registration to full licensing. Individuals keeping bitcoin in their own wallets are outside its scope (anoni.net; LinkedIn/J. Wu).
residency: Taiwan has no simple retirement or nomad visa, but the Employment Gold Card is a realistic route for well-paid professionals. It works as an open work and residence permit for 1–3 years, allows remote work for a foreign employer, costs roughly US$230–300 and usually takes 4–8 weeks. The usual income test is NT$160,000 (about US$5,000) a month (Nomad Tax Guide 2026).
spending: You can buy bitcoin easily, but paying with it in shops is occasional. Exchange BitoPro's payment service BitoPay was set up to let around 300,000 Taiwanese merchants accept bitcoin, but we found little recent evidence of everyday shops actually taking bitcoin (bitcoin.news).

Taiwan Bitcoin Hub hosted the first Bitcoin Squad Asia meetup in Taipei in 2026, bringing together local meetup organisers, wallet teams, educators and node operators from across Asia, and Taiwan has well-known local exchanges and builders (Luma; bitcoin.news).
privacy: Taiwan has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Bitcoin gains are heavily taxed, so you need to declare them yourself, and the tax office can ask for records.

name: Tajikistan

name: Tanzania, United Republic of

name: United Arab Emirates

community: Uruguay has a growing but modest bitcoin community.
privacy: Uruguay has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Uruguay also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Uruguay's rule of law 23rd out of 143 countries, the best in Latin America, and it has a long record of democratic stability. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 43rd of 163 countries.
summary: Uruguay is a calm, well-governed choice with easy residency, good privacy and low tax on income earned abroad. Banks are cautious and the bitcoin scene is still small.

name: Uzbekistan
tax: Under Presidential Decree No. 3832 of 2018, income individuals earn from bitcoin transactions is not taxed and is left out of the tax base. That exemption sits in a decree rather than the tax code, so it could change. (Presidential Decree 3832; Conventus Law)
banking: Residents must buy and sell bitcoin through locally licensed providers, but these connect to local bank cards and payment systems. For example, Binance now serves Uzbekistan through a licensed local company, CoinPay, with deposits and withdrawals in som. Using foreign exchanges is not allowed. (National Agency of Perspective Projects; Times of Central Asia 2025)
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. Bitcoin is allowed only through licensed local providers, and a testing scheme for stablecoin payments started on 1 January 2026 (tradersunion; o2k.tech).
residency: Since 2025, foreigners can buy a 5-year residence permit for about US$200,000. Other routes are work permits or family ties. (Kun.uz; Daryo, April 2025)
spending: Very few places accept bitcoin, as bitcoin payments are tightly controlled. Paying for pizza with bitcoin at Tashkent's Bitcoin Pizza Fest in May 2026 was billed as a first for that event, and stablecoin payments are allowed only in a supervised sandbox from 2026. (Spot.uz 2026; Yahoo Finance 2025)
community: The community is small but growing, with yearly events in Tashkent such as Bitcoin Week Uzbekistan and the Bitcoin Pizza Fest (May 2026). Much of the activity centres on licensed exchanges and trading. (Uzinfocom 2025; Spot.uz 2026)
privacy: Uzbekistan closely monitors financial activity or limits money leaving the country, and bitcoin use is watched or restricted by the authorities.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.50, ranked 81 of 143 countries. Currency: the som has been fairly steady lately, though inflation is still high single digits. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.726, ranked 37 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax. Weakest areas are spending and privacy.

name: Vanuatu
tax: Vanuatu has no personal income tax and no capital gains tax, so individuals pay nothing on bitcoin gains.
banking: Vanuatu has only a few banks, and the main local bank lost its US dollar correspondent link when an Australian bank pulled out, part of a wider Pacific trend of foreign banks cutting ties. No local bank offers bitcoin services yet, so most people buy bitcoin through foreign exchanges or person to person. (Vanuatu Business Review; Pacific Islands Forum correspondent banking report)
legal: Individuals can hold, use and self-custody bitcoin freely. Since the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act of March 2025, bitcoin exchanges, custodians and token issuers must be licensed by the Vanuatu Financial Services Commission, which is phasing in the rules during 2026 and runs a fintech sandbox. (Vanuatu Financial Services Commission; Cointelegraph 2025)
residency: Vanuatu offers one of the cheapest and fastest citizenship-by-investment programmes, from about $130,000.
spending: Paying with bitcoin is rare. Apart from the citizenship programme, which has accepted bitcoin-linked payments, we found no regular shops or restaurants in Port Vila listed as accepting it.
community: The bitcoin scene is very small, made up of a few bitcoin-minded expats and offshore finance workers. The much-publicised Satoshi Island project has government backing, but we found no regular bitcoin meetups in the country. (BTC-Echo; Investing.com)
privacy: Vanuatu has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Vanuatu also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: The vatu is a moderately stable currency and bitcoin policy has been steady, but the country is small and remote. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Vanuatu offers zero tax, very affordable citizenship and good privacy, but banking and everyday bitcoin use are limited.

name: Venezuela, Bolivarian Republic of
tax: Bitcoin is heavily taxed here, or the tax rules are harsh. Bitcoin gains are taxed at up to about 34% (TaxAtlas crypto-tax table 2026).
banking: Most people move between bolivars and bitcoin person to person, especially using the USDT stablecoin, which makes up about 90% of bolivar listings on Binance's person-to-person market. In 2026 some banks, including Banco Plaza and R4, joined an industry working group on digital assets, but banks still offer no regular bitcoin services (BeInCrypto 2026; CriptoNoticias 2026).
legal: Holding and using bitcoin is widespread and tolerated, but the official bitcoin regulator (Sunacrip) has been under a restructuring board since a 2023 corruption scandal, so the rules are unclear. Politics changed after Nicolás Maduro was removed in January 2026, and new rules may follow, so enforcement is unpredictable (CriptoNoticias 2026; BeInCrypto 2026).
residency: Venezuela offers no practical route for foreigners who want to settle there. Immigration services are unreliable, and the security and political situation is still volatile in 2026.
spending: Paying with bitcoin is common in daily life, although it is mostly the USDT stablecoin rather than bitcoin. Many shops, delivery services and freelancers accept bitcoin because of very high inflation, and bitcoin can be spent in parts of Caracas and other cities (BeInCrypto 2026).
community: Venezuela has one of the deepest grassroots bitcoin cultures in the world. Venezuelans made an estimated $17.9 billion of retail bitcoin transactions in early 2026, and local meetups and events are held regularly (TRM Labs via BeInCrypto 2026; CriptoNoticias).
privacy: Venezuela closely monitors financial activity or limits money leaving the country, and bitcoin use is watched or restricted by the authorities.
stability: Unstable: weak rule of law, currency problems or a high risk of sudden changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.26, ranked 143 of 143 countries. Currency: inflation of about 350–400% a year in 2026, the highest in the world. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: government and regulator in transition after January 2026. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.516, ranked 132 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for community. Weakest areas are tax, residency and stability.

name: Viet Nam
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no income tax on bitcoin gains yet (TaxAtlas lists 0%). A proposal would charge 0.1% on each trade on licensed platforms, as for shares (Cointelegraph Mar 2026).
banking: Banking works, but some banks are cautious and transfers may be checked or delayed. Exchanges linked to banks (Techcombank TCEX, VPBank CAEX, LPBank/Sacombank SCEX) are applying under a 5-year pilot scheme, with the first licences expected in Q3 2026. All trading must be settled in dong through designated bank accounts (Cointelegraph; Liminal; bitcoin.news).
legal: Bitcoin is allowed, but the rules are unclear or still being written. The Law on Digital Technology Industry, in force since 1 January 2026, recognises bitcoin assets as property, and a five-year trial for licensed exchanges opened on 20 January 2026. Bitcoin still cannot be used for payment.
residency: Moving here is fairly straightforward if you have a steady income. The digital nomad visa needs about $2,000 a month (destivity).
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin. Bitcoin is not legal for payments in Vietnam, and people mainly use it for investment and sending money home (coinedition/Reuters 2026).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events, and the country ranked 18th of 117 for everyday bitcoin use in Chainalysis's 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index. The everyday bitcoin community is very active, and many people use global exchanges. Attitudes are generally positive among young people and investors, but bitcoin is not yet mainstream in shops (coinledger.io).
privacy: Vietnam closely monitors financial activity or limits money leaving the country, and bitcoin use is watched or restricted by the authorities.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.50, ranked 83 of 143 countries. Currency: moderately stable floating currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.738, ranked 41 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax, residency and community. Weakest area is spending.

name: Virgin Islands, British
tax: The British Virgin Islands has no income tax, capital gains tax or VAT, so bitcoin gains are not taxed.
banking: Bitcoin companies are registered under a 2023 law, but we found no local bank offering bitcoin products to individuals.
legal: Bitcoin businesses have been regulated since February 2023, and individuals are free to use bitcoin.
residency: Moving here is hard for most people. Foreigners normally live in the British Virgin Islands on an employer-sponsored work permit, and the territory is known to be very restrictive about granting permanent "Belonger" status, with the government committing to naturalise no more than 25 people a year. There is no investment or retirement residence programme (Wikipedia: Belonger; BVI Government).
spending: Few shops accept bitcoin. The islands' strength is professional and offshore bitcoin services.
community: The British Virgin Islands has a busy professional bitcoin scene: BVI Finance launched the Fintech on the Seas digital assets conference in 2025 and held it again in June 2026, followed by a free public day on digital assets at the local community college. However, we found no regular grassroots bitcoin meetups, so the everyday community for individual bitcoiners is small and informal. (Government of the Virgin Islands 2026; BVI Finance 2025)
privacy: The British Virgin Islands has signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so from 2028 bitcoin platforms will report customer activity. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the British Virgin Islands, that is the British Virgin Islands's own tax office. Because the British Virgin Islands does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, the reports have little practical effect for residents. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: The islands use the US dollar and operate under English-based law. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: The British Virgin Islands offers zero tax and clear bitcoin rules, but it is better suited to companies than to people looking to move.

name: Virgin Islands, U.S.
tax: The US Virgin Islands use a 'mirror' of the US tax code, so bitcoin is treated as property just as on the mainland: selling or spending it can trigger capital gains tax, at federal-style rates. Residents file their return with the Virgin Islands Bureau of Internal Revenue instead of the IRS, and must report every bitcoin disposal (IRS digital assets guidance; e-file.com Virgin Islands guide).
banking: Banking follows US rules, and the territory's financial regulator has said bitcoin services fall outside its money transmitter rules, which has let US bitcoin infrastructure firms such as zerohash extend services to residents from July 2025. Expect the same strict compliance checks as on the mainland (zerohash, July 2025; Blockspot USVI profile).
legal: Individuals can freely hold, self-custody, spend and trade bitcoin, which the IRS treats as property. The territory has no bitcoin law of its own, so bitcoin businesses are mainly supervised under federal rules and must register with FinCEN as money services businesses (IRS; Blockspot USVI profile).
residency: US citizens can move here freely, but the US Virgin Islands follow exactly the same visa rules as the US mainland. Everyone else needs regular US immigration status, such as a work visa, family sponsorship or a green card, so it is hard for most foreigners (Wikipedia: Visa policy of the United States).
spending: We found no recent reports of shops or restaurants in the islands accepting bitcoin, and local consumer use of bitcoin is described as small. You can still use US online services, but you should not expect to pay with bitcoin in daily life (Blockspot USVI profile).
community: We found no regular bitcoin meetups or local bitcoin groups. Residents interested in bitcoin mostly connect with mainland US communities and events instead (Blockspot USVI profile; meetup searches).
privacy: US federal rules apply here, so bitcoin brokers report trades to the US tax office (IRS). These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the US Virgin Islands, that is the US Virgin Islands's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: US dollar or Swiss franc or fully dollarised – no local-currency risk. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for banking, legal freedom and stability. Weakest areas are tax, residency, spending, community and privacy.

name: Wallis and Futuna
tax: Wallis and Futuna sets its own taxes and has no personal income tax, so residents pay no tax on bitcoin gains. French income tax does not apply to people who genuinely live there. (Decree of 22 July 1957, art. 46; iFRAP; IEOM)
banking: There is only one local bank, the Banque de Wallis et Futuna, plus the post office, and the territory is outside the euro area banking system. Buying bitcoin usually means using a bank account in France or New Caledonia with a European exchange, which can be slow and attract source-of-funds questions. (IEOM 2025)
legal: Owning and using bitcoin is legal. Wallis and Futuna is a French overseas collectivity outside the EU, but French financial and anti-money-laundering rules largely apply, so bitcoin services are regulated while individuals are free to hold and self-custody. (French Monetary and Financial Code; IEOM)
residency: French citizens can settle freely, but other foreigners (including most EU citizens) need a residence permit under the territory's own entry rules, and there is no investor or digital nomad route. Land is held under customary ownership, which makes moving there even harder. (French Overseas Ministry; Wallis and Futuna administration)
spending: We found no shops and no local businesses that accept bitcoin; with about 11,000 people, there is very little commerce of any kind.
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or local groups in Wallis and Futuna. (Meetup listings 2026)
privacy: Wallis and Futuna has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Wallis and Futuna also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Stable, with only a few weak spots. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: the CFP franc is hard-pegged to the euro. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: follows French rules. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for tax and privacy. Weakest areas are spending and community.

name: Western Sahara
tax: Most of the territory is run by Morocco and follows Moroccan rules, where bitcoin transactions have been treated as breaking foreign exchange law since 2017. A draft law (Bill 42.25) to regulate bitcoin was published in November 2025 but is still under review in 2026. (Bank Al-Maghrib; Morocco World News 2026)
banking: Moroccan banks in the territory cannot handle bitcoin under the 2017 ban, and people turn to peer-to-peer trades. (Bank Al-Maghrib; Morocco World News 2026)
legal: Under Moroccan rules, bitcoin transactions are banned as a foreign exchange violation, though Morocco is preparing a law to license bitcoin firms. The territory is also disputed, which adds legal uncertainty. (Morocco World News 2026; Hespress 2025)
residency: In the Moroccan-run area, Moroccan residence rules apply, usually needing a job or family tie. The region is politically sensitive and foreign visitors such as journalists and activists are sometimes expelled. (Moroccan immigration rules; UN reports)
spending: We found no shops that accept bitcoin in Laayoune, Dakhla or elsewhere in the territory.
community: We found no bitcoin meetups or groups in the territory. (Meetup listings 2026)
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Western Sahara, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this territory. Currency: uses the Moroccan dirham, which is pegged to a euro and dollar basket with low inflation. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: Morocco's bitcoin law is still being drafted. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for legal freedom, residency, privacy and stability. Weakest areas are tax, banking, spending and community.

name: Yemen
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banking barely works for bitcoin users. Years of war, US sanctions on Houthi-linked banks (including the International Bank of Yemen in April 2025) and limits on banking apps make transfers slow and unreliable, and a June 2024 central bank circular bans dealings with unlicensed wallets and electronic payment services. Most people who use bitcoin rely on peer-to-peer trades and decentralised apps rather than banks (TRM Labs 2025; The New Arab 2026).
legal: Yemen has no bitcoin law, so owning bitcoin is not explicitly banned, but it sits in a grey area. The central bank has told people not to deal with unlicensed wallets and payment services, and the country is split between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis, with bitcoin linked to the Houthis targeted by US sanctions (Crypto Council for Innovation 2025; TRM Labs 2025).
residency: There is no realistic way for most foreigners to move here. Yemen has been at war since 2014, most governments advise against all travel, and there is no investor, retirement or remote-work residence route (The New Arab 2026).
spending: You will struggle to spend bitcoin in Yemen. Reports mention a few online sellers taking bitcoin, but cash still rules daily life and we found no shops or cafés known to accept bitcoin (The New Arab 2026).
community: Bitcoin use is growing out of necessity, mostly through decentralised apps and peer-to-peer trades used for remittances, and users share know-how through informal networks and diaspora contacts. There are no regular public bitcoin meetups (TRM Labs 2025; Crypto Council for Innovation 2025).
privacy: Bitcoin is restricted in Yemen, and the authorities closely monitor how it is used.
stability: Unstable: weak rule of law, currency problems or a high risk of sudden changes. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: hyperinflation, collapse or no functioning currency. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 3.081, ranked 155 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for tax. Weakest areas are banking, residency, spending and stability.

name: Zambia
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks are cautious. In March 2026 the Bank of Zambia told all bitcoin service providers to register by 27 March. From 30 March, banks may not handle payments to or from providers that have not registered, and they must apply extra checks to bitcoin clients. A full licensing framework is still to come. (Zambia Monitor, March 2026; RegAlert)
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. From 2026 the Bank of Zambia requires bitcoin and stablecoin companies to register (RegAlert crypto regulation guide, July 2026).
residency: Zambia has several routes. An investor's permit needs about 250,000 US dollars to start a business, or 150,000 to join an existing one, and retirees can apply for residence if they prove they have enough money to live on. Work permits need an employer, who usually has to show no qualified Zambian is available. (Visa Atlas; Expat Arrivals)
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. People have been actively adding bitcoin-accepting businesses to BTC Map in 2026 (BTC Map blog).
community: Zambia has a small but growing bitcoin community. BitDevs Zambia started in early 2025 and holds monthly meetups and seminars in Lusaka. It has also run the country's first Lightning developer bootcamp. (BitDevs Zambia on Luma; Nostr post by BitDevs Zambia)
privacy: Zambia has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Zambia also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.45, ranked 103 of 143 countries. Currency: volatile currency with recent devaluation or inflation episodes. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.992, ranked 81 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest area is banking.

name: Zimbabwe
tax: Tax on bitcoin is low, or zero in most everyday cases. There is no specific bitcoin tax, and personal gains are generally not taxed, although frequent trading or business income can fall under general income tax (TaxAtlas 2026).
banking: Banks still keep their distance from bitcoin: a 2018 Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe directive told financial institutions not to process bitcoin payments, so most people buy and sell bitcoin person-to-person, often settling in US dollars or mobile money. A new registration system for bitcoin businesses from 2026 may slowly open more formal routes. (Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe; TaxAtlas 2026; Business Times Zimbabwe 2026)
legal: Bitcoin is legal to hold and trade, and Zimbabwe now has a formal framework: the Finance Act 2025 recognised virtual assets, and Statutory Instrument 99 of 2026 requires bitcoin businesses to register with the Financial Intelligence Unit and follow the travel rule, with licensing by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Individuals are not banned from anything, but the rules are brand new and the central bank's banking restrictions remain. (LEX Africa, September 2026; Business Times Zimbabwe, June 2026)
residency: There is no easy residence route for foreigners. The main options are a work permit tied to a local employer or an investor residence permit, which needs a business plan, proof of funds to invest, police clearance and fees of roughly US$500 to US$1,000. (Zimbabwe Department of Immigration; VisaAtlas 2026)
spending: Only a handful of places accept bitcoin directly. Most everyday bitcoin use is informal, for remittances and swapping with US dollars or mobile money, rather than paying in shops. (TaxAtlas 2026; local reporting)
community: There is a small but real bitcoin community, built around remittances, peer-to-peer trading and online groups, and Zimbabwean voices appear at regional events such as Adopting Bitcoin in Southern Africa. Regular public meetups are hard to find. (Adopting Bitcoin 2026; local reporting)
privacy: Zimbabwe has not signed up to the international bitcoin tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so bitcoin platforms are not set up to report your activity automatically. Zimbabwe also does not tax bitcoin gains for individuals, or taxes them only lightly, so there is little reporting with any practical effect.
stability: Less stable: weaker rule of law, a shaky currency or a risk of sudden policy changes. Rule of law: World Justice Project 2025 score 0.39, ranked 124 of 143 countries. Currency: the ZiG gold-backed currency has brought inflation down to single digits in 2026, but Zimbabwe has a long history of currency collapses and most people still use US dollars. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: a full crypto framework was put in place in 2025 and 2026. Peace and security: Global Peace Index 2026 score 2.051, ranked 89 of 163 countries.
summary: Best for privacy. Weakest areas are banking, residency, spending and stability.

name: Åland Islands
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Finnish rules apply: capital income is taxed at 30% up to EUR 30,000 and 34% above that (Coincub Crypto Tax Report 2025).
banking: Åland uses Finland's euro banking system. Finnish bitcoin providers such as Coinmotion and Northcrypto are now licensed by the Finnish Financial Supervisory Authority under the EU's MiCA rules, so there are reliable regulated ways to buy and sell, though identity and source-of-funds checks are standard (Legal 500 Finland 2025; Northcrypto release May 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. The EU's bitcoin rules (MiCA) have applied in full since 30 December 2024, and national transition periods for existing bitcoin businesses ended by 1 July 2026. You are free to buy, hold, keep in your own wallet and trade bitcoin. EU transfer rules require bitcoin businesses to collect information on transfers to and from personal wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Åland follows Finnish and EU immigration rules: EU citizens can move freely, while others usually need a job, studies or family ties to get a Finnish permit. Åland also has its own 'right of domicile', which requires Finnish citizenship and five years of residence; without it you generally cannot own land or run a business there, except for flats or houses in planned areas or by special permission (Åland Living).
spending: Almost nowhere accepts bitcoin. With about 30,000 residents, we found no evidence of shops on the islands accepting it.
community: We found no local bitcoin meetups or groups. The nearest active communities are in mainland Finland and Sweden.
privacy: Under EU rules (DAC8), bitcoin platforms have reported customer activity to tax offices since 2026. These reports go to the tax office of the country where you are tax resident – if you live in the Åland Islands, that is the Åland Islands's own tax office. Because bitcoin gains are heavily taxed here, the reports are used to check and collect what you owe. Standard identity checks apply when you use exchanges and banks.
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: our estimate, as the World Justice Project does not cover this country. Currency: uses the euro. Risk of a sudden change in bitcoin rules: EU-wide MiCA rules apply. Peace and security: not covered by the Global Peace Index.
summary: Best for stability. Weakest areas are spending and community.
